The rhetorical claim 'high titres against VOCs' conflates binding ELISA (ancestral) with neutralisation (VOC) without distinguishing between them, and the Discussion overstates what the data can support.

Sample sizes are too small for the non-parametric tests used, and pooling across two biological experiments creates pseudo-replication: Two compounding statistical problems. (1) Power: across the immunogenicity (Figs 1-2), chimera (Figs 3-5), and challenge (Figs 6-7) experiments, group sizes are reported as n=2-3 per experiment (totalling 4-6), n=2-6 per chimera arm (the Fig 5 legend explicitly admits n=2-6 even though the prose states n=6), and n=5 for challenge. With Mann-Whitney at n1=n2=3, the smallest achievable two-tailed p is 0.10 — i.e., it is mathematically impossible to reach the conventional α=0.05 in some pairwise tests the paper reports. Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post-hoc on n=4-6 per group has comparably low power, particularly across 4-arm chimera comparisons. No power calculation is reported anywhere in the Methods, and the variable n across panels (n=2-6 vs n=4-6) creates unbalanced post-hoc comparisons whose properties are not discussed. (2) Pseudo-replication: 'individual mice from two independent biological experiments' is treated as the analysis unit, but animals are nested within distinct experiments that differ in vaccine batch, BALF processing day, ELISA plate, pseudovirus prep, and operator. Without an experiment-level random effect (or, equivalently, presenting both experiments separately and showing concordance), the effective degrees of freedom are inflated, standard errors are underestimated, and apparent significance is overstated. The combination of small per-experiment n + pseudo-replication + non-parametric testing makes most reported p-values difficult to interpret.

Reporting gap: no randomisation, blinding, exclusion criteria, sample-size justification, or pre-registered analysis plan (ARRIVE 2.0 noncompliance): ARRIVE 2.0 — the de facto standard for animal-research reporting and a requirement of most journals in this space — calls for explicit reporting of: (a) randomisation method for group allocation, (b) blinding of operators scoring subjective endpoints (clinical score, histology, plaque counts), (c) any animal exclusions and pre-specified criteria for them, (d) the basis of group-size choice (power calculation or pilot data), and (e) a pre-specified primary endpoint and statistical analysis plan. None of these are reported in the Methods. This is particularly consequential here because (i) the clinical score (Fig 6d) is a subjective four-category readout that is highly susceptible to expectancy bias if read unblinded; (ii) the lung histology in Fig 7 reduces to inflammatory cell counts at 'a single 40x field' with no blinded scoring rubric described; (iii) post-hoc test selection (Welch's t vs Mann-Whitney; Dunn's vs Tukey's) is unconstrained by any pre-specified rule, leaving room for p-hacking across many panels. Combined with the absence of any data/code availability statement in Methods, the work is not currently reproducible or independently re-analysable.

Anomalous chimera B-cell increase contradicts the dose-response logic the paper uses elsewhere: Within the paper's own framework, the WT-recipient/WT-donor (WT/WT) and Tlr2-/--recipient/WT-donor (KO/WT BM) groups differ only in TLR2 status of the non-hematopoietic compartment: WT/WT has TLR2 on both compartments, KO/WT has TLR2 only on the hematopoietic side. The KO/WT animals have strictly fewer TLR2-expressing compartments than WT/WT. Yet in this single anomaly, KO/WT shows MORE lung B cells than WT/WT — the opposite of what the additive 'TLR2-dose-response' framework used elsewhere in the paper would predict. The paper does not address this contradiction. Possible explanations include: (i) compensatory upregulation in TLR2-deficient hosts, (ii) radiation/BM-transfer artefact (e.g., differential reconstitution kinetics in Tlr2-/- recipients), (iii) noise from low n. None of these are discussed, but each would substantially weaken the broader claim that TLR2 dose-on-compartments translates monotonically to immune outcomes.

Claim that 'epithelial TLR2 plays a key role' in early APC recruitment is overdrawn from the WT-recipient/KO-donor arm alone: The conclusion that respiratory epithelial TLR2 drives DC, alveolar macrophage and monocyte recruitment rests on the WT-recipient/KO-donor (WT/KO BM) arm at 24 h post a single i.n. dose: this arm shows elevated APC counts vs the KO/KO control. But (1) this arm still contains host-origin radiation-resistant AMs that are themselves TLR2+ tissue-resident immune cells (see major issue on AM radioresistance), so the 'epithelial vs hematopoietic' dichotomy is not cleanly tested by this comparison. (2) 'Respiratory epithelia' is one of several non-hematopoietic compartments that retain TLR2 in WT/KO chimeras — endothelium, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, and resident lung macrophages also express TLR2. The design cannot specifically attribute the recruitment effect to epithelium versus other non-hematopoietic compartments. (3) The Fig 3d effect is at 24 h after a single i.n. dose, but the immunogenicity outcomes the paper most cares about are at 1 wk after three doses; the early innate readout is not shown to causally drive the late adaptive readout (no kinetic chase or perturbation). The phrasing 'plays a key role' should be softened to 'is associated with' unless an epithelial-specific TLR2 conditional KO is used.

ELISA antigen identical to immunogen and lenient cutoff (mean+3SD) inflate apparent antibody titres: Two assay-design issues compound. (1) The Methods do not specify which Spike preparation coats the ELISA plate, but the only recombinant Spike described is the prefusion-stabilised HexaPro construct used for vaccination. If the same HexaPro is the ELISA capture antigen, the assay measures binding to the very conformation the immune system was exposed to, including epitopes specific to the engineered prolines. This systematically inflates titres relative to assays that use native trimer or VOC variants, and over-reports cross-reactivity to wild-type Spike. The ELISA cannot, on its own, support a binding claim against Beta or Delta Spike. (2) The titre cutoff is operationally defined as the dilution interpolating mean+3SD of the unvaccinated 1:100 sera (or 1:40 BALF) — there is no calibration against a reference standard, no assay-validation panel, and no characterisation of inter-plate or inter-day CV. With small unvaccinated reference sample sizes (n=2-3), 'mean+3SD' is itself a noisy estimate. The combination overstates discriminability and biases comparisons across plates and days.

Spike protein endotoxin and aggregate quality not reported despite TLR-driven readouts: Only the PBS is described as endotoxin-tested; the recombinant Spike protein purified from Expi293F cells is not. A TLR4-active LPS contaminant of even low ng/mg amounts in the Spike preparation would directly confound a study whose central claim concerns TLR2-specific adjuvancy: the Tlr2-/- chimera readouts would still receive innate signaling from contaminating LPS via the WT donor compartment (TLR4 is intact). Likewise, gel-filtration step is described, but no analytical SEC trace, percent monomer/aggregate, dynamic light scattering data, or mass-spec confirmation of the prefusion conformation are reported. Aggregated Spike has a different, more potent innate-stimulating profile than monomeric trimer, and could mimic adjuvant-like effects without TLR2 engagement. For a paper that hinges on TLR2-specificity, basic protein-quality and endotoxin reporting are essential.

BM chimera reconstitution efficiency is not verified per animal before vaccination: The chimera design's central inference depends on cleanly dichotomising TLR2 status between hematopoietic and non-hematopoietic compartments. The Methods state a 12-week rest after 800 RAD irradiation and 1.8×10^6 BM cells transfer, but do NOT describe (a) verification of donor chimerism in any tissue (e.g., by CD45.1/CD45.2 flow on peripheral blood pre-vaccination, or by genotyping the Tlr2 locus in blood leukocytes), (b) the percentage donor chimerism considered acceptable, or (c) any animal exclusions for incomplete reconstitution. The Results §2 verification — 'TLR2 expression by FIt-SNE was examined for each experimental group' — is qualitative, group-level, and downstream of the experimental endpoint. Per-animal confirmation that hematopoietic TLR2 status corresponded to the intended chimera condition would substantially strengthen any compartment-attribution claim.

Inconsistent statistical test selection within the same experimental design (Welch's t for Fig 1b, Kruskal-Wallis for Fig 1c-d): Figure 1 has three groups (UNV, s.c., i.n.) with the same n=4-6 per group across panels. Welch's t is a two-group test, so its application to panel (b) implies pairwise testing without an omnibus step (and therefore no correction across the three pairwise contrasts), while panels (c, d) use omnibus Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's correction. The two regimes differ markedly in their type-I error control: Welch's t with no correction is the most permissive, Kruskal-Wallis/Dunn's the most conservative. There is no rationale for switching between them on data from the same experimental design. This pattern of choice — parametric/no-correction where it is favourable and non-parametric/with-correction where it is not — recurs across panels (e.g., Mann-Whitney for Fig 6a, Kruskal-Wallis for Fig 6e-f). Without a pre-specified rule for test choice (e.g., based on Shapiro-Wilk normality), the analysis is selection-biased toward 'significant' calls.

Female-only design across three strains is never disclosed as a generalisability limitation: All cohorts (immunogenicity, chimera, and challenge) are female-only. There is no rationale provided in the Methods, no mention of sex in the Discussion, and no statement of generalisability constraints. Sex-as-a-biological-variable is an explicit NIH/ARRIVE expectation. Mucosal IgA induction, TLR2-driven inflammation, and SARS-CoV-2 disease severity in K18-hACE2 mice are all known to differ between sexes, so a female-only design constrains the conclusions to female mice. The Introduction promises broader population coverage ('young, aged, immunocompromised'), making the silence on sex more conspicuous.

Pseudovirus assay lacks input normalisation and a positive neutralisation control: Several reproducibility-critical parameters are missing from the pseudovirus neutralisation assay used to support the headline nAb titres in Fig 1c. (1) Input pseudovirus titre (e.g., target percentage GFP-positive cells in the no-serum control, TCID50, p24 normalisation, or RLU range) is not specified. EC50 shifts substantially with input dose, so without an input target the absolute titres are not comparable across experiments or to the literature. (2) No positive control (e.g., a reference convalescent serum, a published mAb such as REGN10987 or LY-CoV1404) is used to anchor the assay's potency scale. (3) The ACE2 over-expressing HEK293T line is identified by ATCC catalogue but transduction conditions, ACE2 expression level, and clonal selection are described as 'previously described' rather than re-stated. Without these, reported pseudovirus EC50 values cannot be cross-referenced or independently validated.

Innate (24 h, single dose) and adaptive (1 wk after three doses) chimera readouts cannot be linked to each other in the same animals: The paper's mechanistic narrative is that early innate recruitment (Fig 3, 24 h after a single dose) drives the later adaptive responses (Figs 4-5, 1 wk after three doses) and ultimately the protection (Fig 6, 3 wk after three doses). But these are separate cohorts of animals with different doses, schedules, and timepoints. There is no kinetic measurement, no within-animal pairing, and no perturbation that selectively blocks early innate recruitment to test whether it causally produces the later adaptive readouts. The early innate panel is therefore correlative and descriptive — it cannot, on its own, support a causal role for the early TLR2-mediated APC recruitment in driving the protective immunogenicity. The Discussion uses 'leads to' language ('TLR2 stimulation of the pulmonary epithelia... recruit neutrophils and activate APCs') that overstates what is shown.

Absent CD8+ Spike-specific response leaves the protective mechanism mechanistically incomplete: This is a non-trivial negative finding for a candidate SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. CD8+ T cells are widely considered important for clearing infected airway epithelial cells and for cross-variant protection in scenarios where antibody escape occurs (the same VOC scenario the paper invokes elsewhere). The absence of a Spike-specific CD8+ signal in either lung or spleen — at any of the cytokines screened — has direct implications for the durability and breadth of protection that the abstract and Discussion claim, particularly in the context of 'cross-protection against other pathogenic coronaviruses' the Discussion proposes. The paper reports this finding in a single sentence and does not engage with what it implies (e.g., is the protection antibody-dominant? CD4-only? would the vaccine fail when nAb wanes?). A candidate pulmonary vaccine for a virus where CD8 immunity is increasingly seen as important should at least discuss whether this absence is a concern, an opportunity for additional antigens (NP) as the Discussion mentions in passing, or an artefact of the recall-stimulation conditions.

Discussion's 'future work' list substitutes for honest present-tense limitations: The Discussion enumerates several substantive issues — durability, URT immunity, transmission, prime-pull strategies, hamster/ferret models — exclusively as future work, framed as opportunities rather than as limitations of the present study. This framing matters: stated as future work, these become extensions; stated as limitations, they constrain the current paper's claims. The strongest example is URT immunity: the present manuscript repeatedly motivates mucosal vaccination by URT/transmission control yet measures only lung viral load (see major issue), and the Discussion acknowledges this only by saying future work 'will require an assessment' of URT. A candid limitations paragraph that lists what the data cannot support — 'we did not measure URT viral load and therefore cannot claim transmission-blocking efficacy', 'durability beyond 3 weeks post final dose was not tested', 'protection against Beta or Delta in vivo was not tested', 'the chimera mechanism was not tested in the strain used for protection' — would substantially strengthen the paper's calibration.

Lung IL-17+ CD4+ T-cell skew is presented neutrally without engaging vaccine-enhanced respiratory disease (VERD) literature: An IL-17-dominant lung-resident CD4+ T-cell response is presented as a positive readout. However, prior literature on respiratory viral vaccines — most notably the FI-RSV (formalin-inactivated RSV) catastrophic vaccine trial of the 1960s and several early SARS-CoV vaccine candidates — has flagged Th17/Th2-skewed lung infiltrates as associated with vaccine-enhanced respiratory disease (VERD), characterised by neutrophilic immunopathology on subsequent live virus challenge. The paper does not engage with this concern, despite the present challenge data showing substantial neutrophil influx in BALF (Fig 6e) and inflammatory cell counts in lung histology (Fig 7) even in protected groups. The Discussion's own observation that 'IL-17+ CD4+ T-cell response... is typical following mucosal delivery of protein-based vaccines' should be paired with an explicit statement that VERD risk was monitored for and not observed (with histological criteria), and a discussion of why the IL-17 skew in this model is benign.

Headline 5.4x reduction has 1-sigma lower bound near 1.5, not reflected in abstract: The Abstract reports 5.4x as a definitive number. Section 7 reveals the underlying value is 5.44 ± 3.95 (vs power) and 8.16 ± 6.58 (vs cement). With 1-sigma error bars of 3.95 and 6.58, the lower edge of one standard deviation is approximately 1.5 — i.e., the central claim of dramatic ISI advantage may, within the authors' own uncertainty quantification, reduce to a roughly 1.5x effect. If the ±3.95 represents a 95% CI rather than 1 sigma (the paper does not specify), the lower bound could be below 1, meaning ISI control yields *no greater* TPAE reduction than power control. The abstract's single-point '5.4 times' presentation strips this uncertainty entirely. A faithful summary should report the range or at least flag that the central estimate has a wide uncertainty.

TPAE is presented as health risk but never validated against epidemiological outcomes: The TPAE_{OS} metric is defined as ambient PM_{2.5} concentration multiplied by an in-vitro EC_{1.5}-derived toxic equivalent. There is no demonstrated link between TPAE_{OS} and any clinical or epidemiological endpoint (mortality, hospitalization, lung function). Yet the Abstract and Discussion frame the TPAE reduction as a 'reduction in adverse impacts' and 'health-oriented' control. The Discussion does say 'In vivo and epidemiological studies are strongly encouraged to clarify and validate the relationship', acknowledging the gap, but the paper still presents TPAE as if it were a health metric to support the policy recommendation. Combined with the implicit linear dose-response assumption (TPAE = C × OS, with reductions assumed to scale linearly to harm), this is a meaningful overclaim. A calibrated framing would distinguish 'reduction in toxic-potency-adjusted exposure' (what was measured) from 'reduction in health impact' (which requires further validation).

Static 2017-2022 toxic potency is applied retroactively to 2005-2019 inventory without justification: Field samples were collected 2017-2022, but the OS_{i,s} and CT_{i,s} potencies derived from those samples are applied without modification to the 2005-2019 emission inventory in Fig. 3. The 14-year window encompasses substantial industrial transitions: ISI raw materials and BF/BOF/EAF mix shifted; power-plant coal washing and ULE rollout (post-2014) dramatically changed flue-gas composition; cement clinker chemistry and end-of-pipe controls (ESPs to bag filters) evolved continuously. Each of these would change PM toxicity per gram. The headline narrative 'OS-adjusted emissions increased 12.2% during 2005-2012 even as mass dropped 20%' could be entirely an artifact of holding toxic potency constant. The paper does not perform a sensitivity analysis with time-varying OS_{i,s}, nor does it acknowledge this temporal extrapolation in the limitations paragraph.

OS-adjusted emission share has uncertainty wider than the share itself (70.7 ± 32.9%): 70.7 ± 32.9% means the 1-sigma upper bound is 103.6%, which is mathematically impossible for a fractional share of a sum. Either the uncertainty propagation is incorrect, or the ±32.9% represents Monte-Carlo spread on the absolute OS-adjusted mass that has not been normalized properly to a percentage, or the standard deviation here mixes sample-level variability with share-level uncertainty. As reported, the uncertainty interval cannot reliably distinguish 'ISI ≈ 38%' from 'ISI > 100%' — which would gut the claim that ISI dominates OS-adjusted emissions. The supplement (Suppl. Note 11, Monte Carlo) presumably contains the proper computation, but in the main text the headline number is presented in a form that makes the result unfalsifiable. A more careful statistic (e.g. 5th-95th percentile of the share) should be reported.

PWE/TPAE attribution does not separate 'siting effect' from 'intrinsic potency effect': Population-weighted exposure depends on both the toxic potency of emissions and the spatial overlap between emission sources and population. ISI plants are concentrated in densely populated regions like Hebei and Jiangsu, while power and cement plants have different spatial footprints. The paper attributes ISI's 83% dominance of TPAE_{OS} entirely to 'higher OS potency,' but a fraction of this advantage may be due to ISI's siting near population centers — which is a different policy lever (relocation, fugitive control, urban-rural reallocation) than ULE technology. A decomposition into 'siting effect' vs 'intrinsic potency effect' (e.g. compute TPAE if ISI emissions were spatially distributed identically to power) would clarify how much of the 5.4x advantage is portable to other countries with different industrial geography. Without this decomposition, the policy recommendation is bound to the specific Chinese siting pattern.

Cost-per-OS-adjusted-ton metric is a deterministic transformation of cost-per-mass and OS potency: UCost_OS = ΔTCost / (ΔEmis × OS_{i,s}) = (cost per mass) / OS_{i,s}. Since ISI's OS_{i,s} is 5.0-5.4x larger than power/cement's, the cost per OS-adjusted ton must be roughly 5x lower than the cost per mass — which is exactly what Fig. 5b shows (73%/5.4 ≈ 14%; 142%/5.4 ≈ 26%). Fig. 5b therefore carries no independent information beyond Fig. 1 + Fig. 5a; it is a tautological algebraic consequence of the toxic-potency-adjusted metric definition. Presenting Fig. 5b as separate evidence that 'priority ISI control is more cost-effective for health' overstates the empirical content. The genuinely new information would be the propagated uncertainty on the cost-per-OS-adjusted-ton ratio (combining ΔTCost CI with OS_{i,s} CI), which is not reported.

Single in-vitro model (A549) drives policy conclusion without comparator or threshold sensitivity analysis: All toxic-potency values that drive the policy conclusion derive from one immortalized lung adenocarcinoma cell line (A549). The authors do not justify why A549 is the appropriate model for ranking source-specific PM toxicity, do not include a comparator (BEAS-2B, primary alveolar cells, alveolar macrophages, co-cultures), and do not perform a sensitivity analysis on the EC_{1.5} (1.5-fold ROS) and IC_{20} (20% viability) thresholds. These thresholds materially affect the OS_{i,s} ranking when dose-response curves differ across sectors. The Discussion's generic 'in vitro tests are not strictly consistent with actual exposure' caveat does not address whether ISI's apparent dominance survives a different cell line or threshold choice. Given that the entire policy argument rests on the OS_{i,s} ratio between sectors, a robustness check is essential.

EC_{1.5} sampling at 120°C excludes condensable PM with sector-asymmetric bias: Sampling at 120°C captures filterable PM but excludes condensable material (semi-volatile organics, secondary sulfate/nitrate, volatilized PAHs). This complies with EPA Method 17 for filterable mass, but condensable fractions differ across sectors: power plants with wet FGD have larger condensable sulfate (low intrinsic toxicity per the paper's own framing); ISI sintering may release more condensable PAHs. Whether the 120°C choice biases the cross-sector toxicity ratio upward or downward depends on which sector loses more toxic mass to condensation. The paper does not discuss this in the methods or limitations, even though it directly shapes the headline cross-sector toxicity comparison.

EAF policy recommendation rests on 'limited samples' explicitly admitted by the paper: The Discussion explicitly admits 'limited EAF-emitted PM_{2.5} samples' yet uses the result to recommend a multi-decade industrial transition. The number of EAF samples is not given in the main text. The very next paragraph then says 'The uncertainties in the toxicity of EAF-emitted PM_{2.5} may hinder the evaluation of the effectiveness of current EAF technology' — a direct caveat against the recommendation just made. The two statements appear in adjacent paragraphs and are difficult to reconcile. A more honest framing would mark the BOF-to-EAF shift as a hypothesis to be confirmed with more data rather than a definitive recommendation.

Sample sizes per process and per sector are not reported in the main text: The main text never reports how many units were sampled in each sector (ISI vs power vs cement) or in each sub-process (sinter, pig iron, crude steel, EAF, kiln head, kiln tail, coal/biomass/solid waste boilers). The headline EC_{1.5} ranges have coefficients of variation of 44-57%, but no n is given for any cell, no statistical test (ANOVA, Mann-Whitney, t-test) is reported for cross-sector ratios, and no power calculation is shown. PAH content for ISI is 612 ± 775 μg/g — standard deviation exceeds the mean — yet no median or robust statistic is offered. Without n and tests, the reader cannot judge whether the cross-sector differences are statistically distinguishable from sample-level variability.

Concentration-addition attribution leaves 13-23% of OS unaccounted for and ignores synergy: Targeted metals + PAHs sum to ~87% (ISI), ~87% (power), ~80% (cement). The remaining 13-20% of OS potency is unaccounted for — the paper does not enumerate or quantify what these unidentified contributors are (organic-bound metals, quinones, PAH derivatives, transition-metal speciation). The standard deviation on the ISI metal contribution (±22.6%) is large enough that some samples might have <60% of OS attributable to metals. Additionally, the concentration-addition reference model assumes purely additive mixture toxicity and ignores synergy/antagonism — but in the presence of high Fe (62.6-98.3% of measured ISI metals), redox cycling of Cu, Mn, V, Cr can be enhanced or suppressed via Fenton-type interactions. The Discussion mentions 'synergistic or inhibitory effects ... may generate additional uncertainties' as a generic caveat. A more cautious framing would say 'targeted toxic metals are a leading contributor' rather than 'OS potency could mainly be attributed to PM_{2.5}-bound toxic metals'.

Iron speciation is not measured but is critical to the OS attribution: Iron's contribution to oxidative stress depends on bioavailability, oxidation state (Fe(II) vs Fe(III)), and matrix (haematite vs magnetite vs soluble Fe). The paper aggregates 'total Fe' content into the metal concentration that feeds the OS attribution but never reports speciation. The authors' own ref 33 ('Magnetic Particles Unintentionally Emitted from Anthropogenic Sources: Iron and Steel Plants') indicates magnetite is a dominant ISI emission, and magnetite is *less* redox-active than soluble or amorphous iron oxides. If most ISI Fe is bound as magnetite, the OS attribution may overweight Fe's true ROS contribution. Without speciation data, the metal-driven attribution rests on an untested assumption, and reducing 'Fe content' alone may not reduce ROS as expected — undercutting the policy implication that ISI ULE retrofit translates linearly into health benefit.

WRF-CMAQ model performance metrics are not reported in main text: The paper relies on WRF-CMAQ simulations to compute population-weighted exposure, sector attribution (NoELE/NoCI/NoISI), and ULE-scenario reductions. None of the standard model-performance metrics (NMB, NME, IOA, R for PM_{2.5}) are reported in the main text. Without these, readers cannot assess whether the model is sufficiently skillful for sector-attribution claims like 'ISI accounts for 83% of population-weighted TPAE_{OS}.' Source-attribution sensitivity (e.g., brute-force vs DDM-3D) could give different sector apportionments, especially for primary PM components co-emitted with secondary precursors. At minimum, bulk-PM_{2.5} R^2 and bias should appear in the main text.

Brute-force sector attribution conflates primary and secondary PM contributions: Brute-force source apportionment (zeroing one source at a time) is appropriate for primary PM_{2.5} but does not yield additive contributions when secondary chemistry is non-linear (SO2 → sulfate via OH oxidation, NOx → nitrate equilibrium). For policy targeting *primary* PM_{2.5} from these three sectors, primary-only attribution would be appropriate, but the paper says 'ambient PM_{2.5} concentration attributable to the power, cement, and ISI sectors' — which would normally include secondary sulfate from power-plant SO2 and secondary OC from coke-oven VOCs. If those secondary contributions are bundled in via differencing, the three sector contributions don't sum to a meaningful total. Whether the analysis is primary-only or includes secondary contributions is not stated, which has direct implications for whether ULE retrofits (PM-only) actually deliver the projected reductions.

Stack height, plume rise, and dispersion differences not separated from intrinsic potency effects: Population-weighted exposure depends heavily on stack height and effective plume rise. New Chinese power plant stacks are typically 240 m with significant plume rise; ISI sintering bag-filter stacks are typically 80-120 m. For the same ground-level mass emission, ISI's near-source population dose is generally higher than power's. WRF-CMAQ presumably handles this through layered emission input, but the paper does not quantify whether the TPAE advantage of ISI control is partly due to stack-height-induced near-source exposure rather than intrinsic PM toxicity. If yes, retrofitting power plants in dense urban areas could yield comparable per-mass health benefits because their plume mixes into people's breathing zones differently. A normalization to per-stack effective dose, or a sensitivity analysis fixing all sectors at the same stack height, would isolate the toxicity effect.

Cost calculation excludes variable O&M, retrofit downtime, and labor — likely biased toward ISI advantage: TCost includes only capital, fixed O&M, and fuel costs. Excluded: variable O&M (consumables, sorbents, water for wet ESPs), labor and training cost differences, lost production or downtime during retrofits (especially material for ISI where retrofitting BFs is operationally difficult), end-of-life decommissioning, and compliance/monitoring. The Discussion notes 'implementation of stricter control measures targeting ISI-emitted PM_{2.5} could be a big challenge in the real world because iron and steel production involves complex manufacturing processes' — precisely where the omitted retrofit costs are largest. The under-estimate is therefore likely larger for ISI than for power (which has well-codified ULE retrofit pathways), biasing the cost-effectiveness comparison in favor of ISI prioritization, the headline finding.

ULE attainability for sintering and ironmaking is assumed but not justified: The ISI_ULE scenario assumes 'all facilities in the iron and steel industry meet the ULE levels,' but the main text does not specify the assumed PM_{2.5} emission factor under that scenario. Whether sintering machines (the dominant ISI PM source) can technically achieve power-sector-equivalent ULE limits (~10 mg/m^3) is contested in the literature — wet ESPs and bag filters perform well on power-plant flue gas but face challenges on sinter offgas due to higher temperatures, dust resistivity, and dioxin/heavy-metal content. The ULE attainability assumption is buried in supplementary materials and not justified in the main text, yet it controls the headline 'reduction potential.' If ISI ULE is partial or technology-specific, the projected 36.4% PWE reduction and 5.4x TPAE benefit are upper bounds, not central estimates.

Power ULE baseline assumption inconsistent with reported high pre-2019 ULE rollout: 1000 kt PM_{2.5} reduction implies a large fraction of power plants are NOT yet ULE-compliant in the 2019 baseline. This contradicts widely cited Chinese reports — including the paper's own ref 21 (Tang et al. 2019, Nat. Energy, 'Substantial emission reductions from Chinese power plants after the introduction of ultra-low emissions standards') — which document that >85% of coal capacity met ULE by 2019. If the baseline already incorporates this rollout, the marginal benefit of 'all power plants meeting ULE' should be much smaller than 1000 kt. If the 1000 kt instead represents the cumulative reduction delivered by the rollout from 2014 baseline to 2019 (i.e., 'no-ULE 2014 + 5 years of growth' counterfactual minus 'actual 2019'), the comparison to ISI's 621 kt 'fully-deployed ULE' projection is apples to oranges. The exact baseline assumption underlying the 1000 kt is not made explicit in the main text.

Fugitive ISI emissions are not measured but are likely a substantial fraction of total ISI PM: ISI plants are not single-stack sources — sintering, BF, BOF each have multiple stack and fugitive sources (sinter cooler, BF cast house, BOF charging/tapping/secondary fume, slag handling, raw-material yards). The paper measures stack PM via isokinetic sampling, but a major fraction of ISI PM is fugitive. Fugitive emissions tend to be richer in iron oxides and depleted in PAHs, with potentially lower OS potency than stack samples. If the inventory's ISI emission factor includes fugitive sources but the toxic potency is derived only from stack samples, ISI's TPA emission is overestimated (higher mass × inappropriately high unit potency). The Discussion mentions fugitive aerosols generally but does not quantify the bias direction.

Headline '~2 times higher than the previous decade' compares compound (heat+COVID) mortality to heat-only baseline: The Abstract attributes the 19-24/100k heat and 80-127/100k cold figures to compound (extreme temperatures + COVID-19) effects, then states they are '~2 times higher than the previous decade.' But the body text shows the comparison is between (heat+COVID) in 2020-2022 and (heat alone) in 2010-2019. Any non-trivial COVID-19 share alone produces a ratio >1 even if temperature mortality is unchanged. In Figure 2c (cold snaps), COVID-19 dominates: temperature-to-COVID ratios are 0.4-0.8, meaning 55-71% of the 80-127/100k cold-snap compound figure is actually COVID-19, not cold. The 1.7-3.8x heat fold-change and 2.1-3.5x cold fold-change therefore conflate two distinct effects (modest heat increase + addition of COVID-19) without decomposition. A reader naturally infers temperature mortality alone roughly doubled, which is not what the data show. A like-for-like decomposition is missing.

Independence assumption used to compute compound mortality is contradicted by the paper's own evidence of confounding: All headline compound mortality figures (Figures 3a-b; abstract values) are computed under explicit additive independence. The Results then present Figure 4 and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests as evidence that 'COVID-19 may have impacted temperature-related mortality,' and the Discussion strengthens this to 'COVID-19 may have confounded with temperature-related mortality' and even asserts that mortality impacts are 'additive to the first order, are clear in this paper.' These positions are mutually inconsistent: if independence holds, the Figure 4 K-S evidence is misinterpreted; if it fails, the additive compound numbers are biased and the bias direction/magnitude must be quantified. Currently both narratives are presented as valid, which they cannot simultaneously be.

DLNM fit on 1981-2022 mortality with COVID-19 deaths surgically removed creates structural bias and circular reasoning: The dependent variable is conditioned on COVID-19 cause-of-death coding only for 2020-2022, creating a structural break unique to that period. Three problems follow: (i) deaths with COVID-19 'on the certificate' include cases where COVID-19 was incidental, while many true COVID-19 deaths in early 2020 were uncoded due to testing limitations; (ii) the temperature-mortality association estimated this way is contaminated by COVID-19 INDIRECT effects (e.g., disrupted healthcare causing excess CVD on hot days); (iii) the authors then interpret the residual as 'temperature-related' and treat distributional shifts in this residual as evidence of COVID-19 confounding (Figure 4) — circular. The Discussion's own recommendation to 'derive temperature-mortality associations using only data from the COVID-19 time period' implicitly concedes that pooling 1981-2019 with 2020-2022 (with COVID deaths removed) produces biased estimates for 2020-2022. A cleaner approach would be to either fit on 1981-2019 only and project, or include a COVID-19 indicator/spline in the model.

Heatwave and cold-snap definitions are inconsistent across the 2010-2015, 2016-2022, and 2020-2022 windows despite being claimed as 'same criteria': For 2016-2022, heatwaves come from UKHSA Heat Mortality Monitoring Reports and cold snaps from Level 3 Cold Health Alerts (a forecast-based trigger). For 2010-2015, heatwaves use 'Level 3 Heat Health Alert OR mean Central England Temperature >20°C plus 1-day buffer,' and cold snaps use 'any region <2°C for 2+ consecutive days.' The CET >20°C criterion uses a single Midlands-region temperature index to define heatwave days for all 10 regions, including Wales, which is outside the CET footprint. The 'any region' rule for cold snaps means days are counted as cold-snap days for regions that themselves were not below 2°C. These four definitions select different sets of days under different physical thresholds, undermining the headline '~2x previous decade' fold-change calculation in Figure 3 (a vs c, b vs d). The claim of 'same criteria' is incorrect.

Asymmetric region-pooling rule for cold snaps inflates 'cold-snap days' relative to heatwaves: Cold snaps are defined as days when a Level 3 Cold Health Alert was issued for ANY region in England — meaning a region under no alert is still counted as a 'cold-snap' region for those days. There is no equivalent 'any region' rule applied to heatwaves. This asymmetry inflates the cold-snap denominator for less-affected regions, dilutes per-day cold-mortality estimates, and produces a non-comparable ratio against heatwaves. It also affects the per-100k compound mortality numbers in Figure 3b (cold) but not Figure 3a (heat), introducing a systematic bias into the central heat-vs-cold comparison.

K-S tests in Figure 4 cannot separate COVID-19 confounding from sampling differences in event severity: The K-S test detects a distributional shift but cannot distinguish (a) 'COVID-19 amplified mortality at given temperatures' from (b) '2020-2022 events were more extreme.' The text itself notes mean heatwave temperature shifted higher in 2020-2022 (consistent with the 40.3°C UK record being set then). With ~10 heatwaves and ~8 cold snaps in 2020-2022 versus ~4 years of pre-COVID events (2016-2019), per-region samples for the bivariate (mean temperature, mortality/day) comparison are very small. The K-S test as described is univariate; how it is applied to the bivariate space is not specified. Multiple-comparisons correction across regions and event types is not reported. Despite these limitations, the Discussion treats the result as a key piece of evidence for the 'COVID-19 as risk amplifier' hypothesis. The Discussion's own caveat ('the number of extreme temperature events sampled is limited by the short study period') does not appear at the point of the K-S claim in Results.

Paper holds prior weather-COVID literature to a methodological standard it does not apply to its own COVID-19 mortality claim: The paper approvingly cites Tan & Schultz (2023) for finding that prior weather-COVID studies failed to include a lag, account for seasonality, or control confounders. Yet the present paper's claim that 'extreme heat may have exacerbated COVID-19 mortality' (supported by '91 more daily COVID-19 deaths' on 19 July 2022 versus the 10-25 July 2022 mean, Figure 1b) uses zero-lag, single-day data with no statistical test, no seasonality control beyond a 2-week window, and no adjustment for day-of-week reporting effects in COVID-19 death certificates. The paper applies a stricter standard to others than to itself, weakening the credibility of its own causal claim.

'Demand on regional health services was 1.7 to 3.8-fold' conflates mortality counts with service load: Mortality counts are not a proxy for health-service demand. A typical COVID-19 death follows extended hospitalization (often ICU), while heat-related deaths are frequently acute cardiovascular events with shorter or absent hospitalization. Equating them implicitly assumes per-death service load is uniform, which is unsupported. The 1.7-3.8x figure thus does not measure what its label claims. This matters because the Discussion uses the figure to argue that NHS bed shortages compounded with these mortality numbers to overwhelm the system — an argument that requires a service-load metric, not a mortality metric. The paper should reframe the language as a mortality fold-change, not a demand fold-change, or supply data on per-death healthcare utilization.

Headline cold-snap compound mortality (80-127/100k) is overwhelmingly driven by COVID-19, not cold: Figure 2c shows that during cold snaps, the ratio of cold-related to COVID-19 deaths is 0.4 (East of England) to 0.8 (South West) — meaning COVID-19 contributes 56-71% of the compound figure. The framing as 'compound (cold-related and COVID-19) mortality' obscures that cold is the smaller share, not the dominant one. The cold/heat comparison ('cold-snap compound is 5-7x larger than heatwave compound') is therefore mostly a comparison of when COVID-19 mortality was high (winter) versus low (summer of 2022), not an extreme-temperature severity comparison. This asymmetry between the heat and cold regimes — heat compound numbers are dominated by heat (ratios 1.1-2.7 except NW), while cold compound numbers are dominated by COVID — is not made explicit anywhere in the paper.

Heatwave and cold-snap windows both span exactly 70 days — implausible coincidence with no methodological explanation: Ten heatwaves under one definition and eight cold snaps under a different definition coincidentally span exactly the same number of days (70). The text gives no explanation. If one period was truncated to match the other for comparability, that truncation rule should be stated since cold snaps are typically several days long and the cutoff materially changes which days are counted. If the equality is coincidental, that should be noted. As written, this is an unjustified design choice that affects all per-100k compound mortality numbers in Figures 3a-b.

Number of heatwaves and cold snaps in the 2010-2019 reference is never stated: The 2010-2019 reference uses 'the average of all identified heatwaves' scaled to 70 days, but the count of heatwaves and total heatwave-days in 2010-2019 is not given. A reader cannot evaluate whether the per-day average is stable, whether the 70-day extrapolation is dominated by a single event (e.g., the August 2003 or July 2018 heatwaves), or whether the same number of days were available for both periods. The same applies to cold snaps. This transparency gap directly affects the headline '~2x previous decade' comparison.

Selection of 8% exceedance in South West England as headline obscures that the other 9 regions are below 100%: Of 10 regions, only South West crosses the 100% threshold. The body reports that other regions ranged from 58% (East Midlands) to 75% (London) of COVID-19 deaths. Highlighting the single region where exceedance occurred — without stating the range — risks creating an impression that this is a typical or near-universal pattern. A more accurate framing would convey the full distribution (ratios 0.58-1.08 across regions). Additionally, SW being roughly 1.5x London on this metric (108% / 75%) is a large discontinuity that the paper does not explain, leaving readers unable to evaluate whether the SW result is robust or driven by an idiosyncratic regional feature (e.g., relatively low COVID-19 burden combined with relatively warm climate).

Discussion misuses cited UCL forecast (window: through May 2024) to support a '2 to 5 year' extrapolation, with supporting analysis 'not shown': The cited COVID-19 forecast (ref 37) extends 'until at least May 2024,' a window of months. The Discussion extrapolates to '2 to 5 years' of dominance of temperature-related deaths. The supporting analysis is described only as '(not shown).' A forward-looking claim that drives a policy recommendation should not rest on (a) extrapolation well beyond the forecast horizon and (b) an unshown calculation. Either include the analysis or downgrade the claim.

Single-day anecdote (91 extra COVID-19 deaths on 19 July 2022) used as causal evidence with no statistical test: A single-day anomaly is presented as 'evident' support for a causal claim. Multiple alternative explanations are not addressed: (i) reporting/death-certificate timing artifacts, since reported deaths often correspond to deaths registered earlier; (ii) day-of-week effects in COVID death reporting; (iii) random variation in a noisy daily count. With no statistical test, no comparison to other heatwave days, and no consideration of reporting lag, the 'evident' framing is too strong. There is also a grammatical artifact ('the 91 more daily COVID-19 deaths') suggesting an editing slip.

Methods do not state how confidence intervals are computed for compound mortality (sum of temperature-related and COVID-19 deaths): The Methods describe CIs for temperature-related mortality only. The compound mortality reported in Figure 3a-b (e.g., 19-24/100k heat) is presumably the sum of temperature-related deaths and COVID-19 deaths, but the paper does not state how the CI of the sum is computed. If COVID-19 death counts are treated as exact (no uncertainty), the compound CI inherits only DLNM uncertainty — appropriate only if ONS COVID-19 death certificate counts are treated as ground truth. The Discussion explicitly notes uncertainty in cause-of-death coding for COVID-19, which would propagate into the compound CI. As reported, the compound CIs in Figure 3a-b may be too narrow.

Only 100 Monte Carlo draws are used for 95% empirical CIs, well below the field standard: Empirical 95% CIs from 100 draws have substantial Monte Carlo error: the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles correspond roughly to the 3rd and 98th order statistics with non-trivial sampling variability. The DLNM tutorial cited (ref 58, Vicedo-Cabrera et al. 2019) demonstrates with 1,000+ draws. This affects the reported CIs (e.g., 6,387-10,493 for 8,481 heat deaths) particularly at the bounds. Several headline claims depend on whether per-100k mortality CIs overlap between regions or between 2020-2022 and 2010-2019.

MMT constraint to 2nd-98th percentile and asymmetric knot placement (10/75/90) are non-standard and unjustified: Two related design choices in the DLNM specification go unjustified. First, the MMT is constrained to the 2nd-98th percentile of regional 1981-2022 temperature, while standard practice (e.g., Gasparrini et al. 2015, ref 27) uses 1st-99th. With more aggressive truncation, MMT can be pushed inward, miscategorizing borderline temperatures as 'heat' or 'cold' that would otherwise be optimal. Second, the spline knots at 10/75/90 percentile give more flexibility on the upper tail than on the lower tail, but the cold-mortality estimates (15x larger than heat) depend strongly on shape estimates well below the 10th percentile, where extrapolation is determined by knot placement and boundary conditions. Neither choice is justified, and no sensitivity analysis is reported. (Note: the printed '2^{th}' is also a typographical error.)

Acknowledged contradiction with Thompson et al. 2022 (ref 51) is dismissed in one sentence without methodological reconciliation: The Discussion notes Thompson et al. 2022 (ref 51) found similar heatwave mortality in 2020 and 2016-2018, contradicting the present paper's confounding hypothesis. This is mentioned in one sentence without engaging with the methodological differences (model specification, geographic granularity, time window, mortality dataset version). Notably, ref 51 includes an author who is also cited (ref 23) as part of the modeling lineage that the present paper builds on. The discrepancy with overlapping prior work deserves more than a sentence; the failure to reconcile undermines the strength of the paper's contribution to the literature debate.

Novelty claim 'no study has quantified the compound health consequences' is contradicted by cited work (Sousa 2022, ref 50): The Abstract claims novelty as the first quantification of compound climate-pandemic health consequences. But the paper itself cites Sousa et al. 2022 (ref 50), 'Heat-related mortality amplified during the COVID-19 pandemic' in Portugal, which already quantifies one dimension of compound effects. Lo et al. 2022 (ref 23) provides the modeling apparatus for E&W. Thompson et al. 2022 (ref 51) examines 2020 heatwave mortality in England relative to pre-pandemic. The novelty claim is therefore overstated. A more accurate statement would specify the novel scope (e.g., 'first to combine heat AND cold AND COVID-19 in regional E&W' or similar).

Date errors in the discussion of the July 2022 heatwave: The text gives '11 July 2021' and '18 July 2021' for the alerts surrounding the 19 July 2022 record. The years should be 2022, not 2021 (UKHSA's first-ever Level 4 Heat Health Alert was declared 18 July 2022). A separate sentence contains 'highest daily mortality level being 1,382 deaths on 19 Janurary 2021' (typo for 'January'), and the placement of the dotted vertical line at 'the domination of the Alpha variant in December 2020' is questionable since Alpha became dominant in the UK in early 2021. These chronological errors undermine reader trust in the time-series narrative around the headline events.

All-cause mortality comparison to '2010-2019' is not adjusted for population growth or aging: The claim that all-cause mortality in 2020-2022 was higher than in 2010-2019 is made without specifying magnitude or controlling for demographic change. The over-65 population in England and Wales grew substantially over 2010-2022, and population aging alone increases all-cause mortality. The 2010-2019 baseline (used for the error bars in Figure 1a) is not explicitly age-standardized in the description. Without standardization, attributing the elevated all-cause mortality to compound impacts of temperatures+COVID-19 conflates the demographic trend with the pandemic/extreme-weather effect.

Cumulative ratio comparison is sensitive to study-window endpoints, but no sensitivity analysis is reported: The cumulative ratio over a 35-month window mixes the pre-vaccine pandemic (high COVID-19 mortality) with post-vaccine periods (low COVID-19 mortality). The ratio is highly sensitive to start and end dates: starting on 30 January 2020 captures the first wave at full force, while ending on 31 December 2022 includes a long post-vaccination tail of low COVID-19 mortality. The headline '8% exceedance in South West' is a single percentage point above 100% and could plausibly flip with small shifts in the window. No sensitivity analysis to study-period choice is reported.

Decomposition results: scenario labels swapped between §2.3 and §4, with at least one impossible reused CI: The central decomposition results are internally inconsistent. (1) §2.3 reports SSP1-2.6 aging = 674k and SSP5-8.5 aging = 703k, but §4 (Conclusions) gives the same two scenarios as 718-746k and 608-656k. The 718-746 range matches §2.3's reported SSP2-4.5 (730k, 718-746) and 608-656 matches §2.3's SSP3-7.0 (634k, 608-656) — i.e., the Conclusions appear to mislabel which scenarios are being summarized, the very claim that 'aging is the only positive contributor in SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5'. (2) §2.3 also reports the disease-mortality reduction for SSP2-4.5 as '658(608-656, 95%CI) thousand' — the CI '608-656' is identical to that of the SSP3-7.0 aging contribution stated in the same paragraph. Two unrelated decomposition outputs cannot share an identical 95% CI to the unit; this is a copy-paste/labeling error. Together these errors mean the headline claim about which scenarios are 'aging-only' rests on numbers the paper itself reports inconsistently.

Per-annum vs cumulative units error makes aging contribution figures internally impossible: §2.3 says aging produces increases of 674k DAPP 'per annum' for SSP1-2.6 (and 703k for SSP5-8.5). If 'per annum' is taken literally — 18 years × 674k/year ≈ 12 million extra deaths from aging alone — this would dwarf the net DAPP changes (-32k to -178k over the entire 2017-2035 horizon) by two to three orders of magnitude. The intended meaning is cumulative 2017-2035, not annual. This units error is likely the source of several other anomalies (e.g., 'DAPP per capita 855 per 10,000' in Northeast China, which would imply ~8.55% annual mortality from PM2.5 — physically impossible). The paper consistently switches between cumulative-period decomposition contributions and per-year mortality without flagging the change.

PM2.5 calibration formula (Eq. 5) is mathematically circular and uninterpretable as printed: The bias-correction formula that translates raw CMIP6 PM2.5 reconstructions to the values used for all DAPP projections is uninterpretable. The variable PM_{2.5 mod x} appears on both the LHS and inside the RHS numerator, with a superscript that may be either a power or an OCR-rendered minus sign. The accompanying text defines PM_{2.5 mod x} as 'the PM2.5 concentration obtained according to equation 5' — i.e., circularly. The intended Chowdhury/van Donkelaar-style correction is presumably PM_calibrated_x = PM_obs_bl × (PM_mod_x / PM_mod_bl), but Eq. (5) as printed cannot be reproduced. Since downstream PM2.5 projections — and therefore every reported DAPP figure — depend on this calibration, this is a critical reproducibility gap.

Composite uncertainty rule for DAPP confidence intervals not specified: Three independent uncertainty sources feed the DAPP CI: the MR-BRT exposure-response (1000 posterior draws), the PM2.5 concentration (CMIP6 multi-model t-distribution with 11 models), and disease mortality (Foreman ARIMA residuals). The paper never describes how they are combined. Naive worst-case bounds, RSS combination, and Monte Carlo propagation give materially different intervals. Every 95% CI in the paper — including the abstract's 31.9 (26.6-45.6) to 178.8 (152.5-210.5) thousand range, the '95% in Northeast China' claim, and the '>98% from aging' decomposition shares — depends on this missing combination rule. Combined with the apparently incorrect prediction-variance formula in Eq. (11) and the singular 'the 1000th curve fit' phrasing, the CIs as reported cannot be independently validated.

Eq. 11 prediction-variance formula is not the standard OLS prediction-interval form: The standard OLS prediction-interval variance at a new point x_f is σ²·[1/n + (x_f − x̄)² / Σ(x_i − x̄)²], using a *sum* of squared deviations and *adding* the two leverage terms. As printed, Eq. (11) (i) shows (x_i − x̄)² without a Σ in the denominator, and (ii) multiplies (×) the two leverage terms rather than adding (+) them. As literally printed, the formula yields incorrect — and likely much smaller — variances. This affects every reported disease-mortality CI, which propagates into every DAPP CI. Either the formula is mis-typeset (in which case the corrected version should be substituted) or the implementation followed the printed form, in which case the entire CI structure is anti-conservative.

Decomposition tables labeled 'PM10 concentration' although the analysis is about PM2.5: The header row of all three provincial driver-decomposition tables (tbl-0/tbl-1/tbl-2 under Figure 4) reads 'PM10 concentration contribution', whereas the entire study quantifies and decomposes deaths attributable to PM2.5. Methods Eq. (3) reconstructs PM2.5 from CMIP6 species (BC + OA + SO4 + NH4 + 0.25*SS + 0.1*dust), and the exposure-response function (MR-BRT) is for PM2.5. PM10 has a different exposure-response function. Either this is a typo (likely), in which case it should be corrected because PM10 vs PM2.5 mortality is not interchangeable for downstream readers; or the decomposition actually used PM10 anywhere, which would be a major methodological inconsistency.

Headline 'aging offsets gains' claim applies only to 2025-2035 sub-period, not 2017-2035: The abstract states aging will 'offset the positive gains' — implying net DAPP rises. But §2.2 shows net 2017-2035 DAPP DECLINES in three of four scenarios (-32 to -178k); the only periods in which aging actually drives net growth are 2025-2035 (and only in three scenarios), with 2017-2025 dominated by disease-mortality declines. The abstract therefore overstates the temporal scope of the central finding. The accurate framing is 'beginning in 2025, aging becomes the dominant positive driver and largely offsets continuing gains, but net DAPP still declines by 2035 in three of four scenarios'. As written, a casual reader would conclude aging causes net DAPP rises across the whole period.

Abstract restricts headline DAPP range to three of four scenarios, omitting SSP3-7.0: The paper's analysis covers four CMIP6 scenarios; §2.2 and §4 give DAPP changes for all four. The abstract excludes SSP3-7.0 (regional rivalry) without explanation — yet SSP3-7.0 is the only scenario in which population-weighted PM2.5 *rises* (to 43.33 µg/m³) and one of two scenarios in which net DAPP grows after 2025 (+72k from 2025-2035). Excluding the highest-DAPP scenario from the abstract's reported range materially understates the message of the paper to a reader who reads only the abstract.

Conclusions report scenario ranges as cherry-picked CI bounds rather than point-estimate ranges: Section 2.2 gives 2017-2025 declines of 132/71/26/118k for SSP1/2/3/5 (point-estimate range 26-132) and 2025-2035 increases of 37/72/24k for SSP2/3/5 (range 24-72). The Conclusions instead state 'decline by 19-146 thousand' and 'increase by 19-81 thousand'. The 19, 146, and 81 values do not correspond to any scenario point estimate — they correspond to the lowest lower 95% CI bound and highest upper 95% CI bound across scenarios. Reporting these as a range conflates CI bounds across different scenarios in a way that misleadingly widens the apparent range. The Conclusions should give either point-estimate ranges or the range of CIs per scenario.

Per-capita DAPP figures (e.g., '855 per 10,000') incompatible with annual mortality: 855 deaths per 10,000 people (per year) implies an 8.55% annual mortality rate from PM2.5 alone — exceeding total all-cause crude mortality in China (~7-8 per thousand annually). This is physically impossible if interpreted as an annual rate. The decomposition tables earlier give per-capita DAPP changes in a plausible range (-3 to +7 per 10,000), so the units differ between sections without explanation. The most likely interpretations are (a) cumulative DAPP over 18 years per 10,000 baseline population, or (b) DAPP per 10,000 in some restricted age group. Either way, the unit needs to be made explicit.

Heilongjiang absolute DAPP increases stated in main text are an order of magnitude larger than table values: The decomposition tables show Heilongjiang per-capita DAPP changes of +0.1, +0.57, +0.96, +0.31 (per 10,000 people) across scenarios. With a Heilongjiang population of ~38 million, +0.1 per 10,000 implies ~380 added deaths, +0.57 implies ~2,170, +0.96 implies ~3,650, +0.31 implies ~1,180. The text claim of 10,000/6,000/10,000/3,000 is roughly an order of magnitude higher. This is a key example used to support the Northeast-China-grows claim, and readers cannot reconcile it with the tables. Combined with the per-annum/cumulative confusion, the magnitudes the paper presents are not internally derivable.

Six diseases listed in methods but Figure 5 caption omits stroke: Methods Eq. 1 and the discussion repeatedly state DAPP is computed for six diseases (COPD, DM2, IHD, LC, LRI, stroke). The text immediately above Figure 5 explicitly names six. But Figure 5's caption — the figure that purports to show the proportion of deaths by disease — lists only five. Stroke is a leading PM2.5-attributable cause and its omission from the figure caption is unlikely to be incidental. Either Figure 5 plots only five (in which case the central 'aging dominates by disease' claim has missing data) or the caption is wrong (still an error in a key supporting figure).

Region-to-income mapping in §3.2 narrative conflicts with Table 1: §3.2 narrative classifies Chinese regions as low-income (Central, West), upper-middle (Northeast), and high-income (East). Table 1 in the same section uses different groups: 'East, South' high-income, 'North, Northeast' upper-middle, 'Central, Northwest' lower-middle. The narrative mentions West China but not Northwest, treats Northeast as upper-middle alone (not jointly with North), and omits North/South from the typology entirely. Additionally, Table 1 lists the elderly proportion of 'East, South' as 22.2% — close to U.S./Japan's 22.5% — but the introduction projects China's overall 65+ share at only 17.1% by 2030 and 26.3% by 2050. East China is among the more aged Chinese regions, but a current 22.2% would be implausible without a labeled time horizon. Together these inconsistencies make the international-insight comparison hard to verify.

Methods describe three-period decomposition but Results report only two: Methods §5.2 explicitly state the decomposition was performed for three sub-periods (2017-2025, 2025-2030, 2030-2035), but the Results consistently report only two intervals (2017-2025 and 2025-2035). The 2025-2030 vs 2030-2035 split — likely the most informative for showing aging's accelerating dominance — is never presented. Either the methods description is inaccurate or important results are omitted from the main text without explanation.

Population data integration between Jiang et al (gridded) and Chen et al (provincial age structure) not described: Two distinct projection products are used: Chen et al. (ref 48) provides provincial age structure, while Jiang et al. (ref 47) provides 0.5° gridded total population. The two datasets are built with different assumptions about fertility, mortality, and migration trajectories under the SSPs and need not agree even at the provincial total level. The paper never explains how they are reconciled — does the gridded Jiang population get rescaled to match Chen provincial totals? Are Chen age fractions applied directly to gridded Jiang totals? Mis-pairing biases both the AgeP_a term in Eq. (1) and the population term in the decomposition, but the procedure is unspecified.

PM2.5 reconstruction Eq. (3) coefficients (0.25 SS, 0.1 dust) lack provenance and a sensitivity analysis: Equation (3) reconstructs PM2.5 from CMIP6 species concentrations using factors 0.25 for sea salt and 0.10 for dust, representing the mass fraction in the fine size range. These factors come from Chowdhury et al. and van Donkelaar et al., but the paper does not state this and does not assess whether they hold across the 11 different CMIP6 models with their varying sea-salt size bins and dust resolutions. The constants could introduce systematic biases up to a factor of 2 in arid northwestern provinces, where dust dominates aerosol mass and where the provincial PM2.5 + aging story is most sensitive. No sensitivity analysis is presented.

DAPP excludes deaths in <25 age group without justification, and excludes household air pollution without quantifying the bias: Two related scoping decisions are made without justification. (1) DAPP is computed only for ages ≥25, excluding child LRI deaths which GBD 2019 attributes meaningfully to ambient PM2.5 in low-and-middle-income contexts. Restricting to ≥25 raises the elderly's relative DAPP share by construction. (2) Indoor (household) PM2.5 is excluded entirely — the methods note this and that GBDMAPS (which includes indoor) reports higher DAPP. Household PM2.5 produces ~2.3M global deaths/year (GBD 2019) and disproportionately exposes rural elderly via solid-fuel cooking and heating in winter. The paper's central claim is about elderly vulnerability; excluding indoor exposure systematically biases that very claim. Both decisions deserve explicit justification or sensitivity tests.

Validation by Pearson correlation cannot detect bias; magnitudes diverge in the paper's own comparison: Pearson correlation measures linear association, not magnitude agreement. Two methods can correlate at r=0.99 while one consistently produces 50% higher values. The paper later explicitly notes 'estimates based on the GEMM model were higher than our estimates' — a systematic bias Pearson cannot detect. Reporting only Pearson is a self-consistency standards issue: the paper recognizes magnitudes diverge across methods but the validation step never quantifies this. RMSE, mean bias, or Lin's concordance correlation should be reported with calibration scatterplots.

Ambiguous '190%/120%/110%/90%' growth in elderly proportion across SSPs: The figures are presented without an explicit base or unit. Read as percentage-point increases on top of China's 2017 ~11% elderly share, they would mean elderly shares in 2035 of ~31%/23%/22%/21% — implausibly large for a 13-year horizon (UN/Chen et al. SSP projections give ~17-21% by 2035). Read as relative percent increases (~110% means roughly doubling), SSP5-8.5 at +190% would still mean tripling the elderly share to ~32% by 2035 — also implausibly large. The paragraph supports the central thesis (population aging is the dominant DAPP driver), so a clearly-stated base/unit is essential. Either the figures are wrong or the prose is misleading.

Aging-share denominator (the '70%/95% caused by aging' claim) is not specified: In SSP1-2.6, §2.3 says aging is the *only* positive driver — so 100% of the growth-causing contribution is aging. The text instead reports '>70%' and '95% in Northeast China'. If the denominator is total positive contributions, the SSP1-2.6 fraction should be 100%, not 70%. If the denominator is gross |positive| + |negative| absolute contributions, the resulting fraction is not interpretable as 'growth caused by aging'. Likewise, for Heilongjiang (the most-aged province), the decomposition shows an age-structure positive contribution (~3.1) competing with disease-mortality (-2.0) and PM2.5 (-0.7) negatives, and a small population effect; whether this gives '95%' aging share depends entirely on the denominator. The paper should make the percentage formula explicit.

Discussion 3.1 paraphrases §2.3's '80% of total DAPP' as '80% of total deaths of all ages': Section 2.3 reports: 'the average proportion of older people dying from six diseases ... will account for more than 80% of the total DAPP' — i.e., elderly DAPP is >80% of total DAPP from these six diseases. Discussion 3.1 paraphrases this as '80% of the respective total deaths of all ages' — a different claim (it would mean 80% of all DM2/IHD deaths from any cause are in the elderly, which is demographically plausible but is not what §2.3 says). Slipping the denominator from 'PM2.5-attributable deaths' to 'all-cause deaths' is a substantive over-extension of the supporting evidence.

Conclusions about freely-behaving in-vivo deep-brain fiber photometry are not supported by the bench-only experiments: Every experiment in the paper is on a coverslip or a fixed (post-mortem) 50 um brain slice with DMD-controlled excitation; the miniscope+fiber test uses only a single bead. There is no in-vivo recording, no implantation, no awake-animal data, and no demonstration of fiber bending, motion, or chronic stability. Yet the abstract suggests 'a whole new avenue for novel minimally invasive deep brain studies with multimode fibers in freely-behaving mice is possible' and the conclusion projects to multi-region freely-behaving deep-brain experiments. This is a substantive overgeneralization from bench data; the paper-level conclusions need to be scoped to what is actually demonstrated, with the freely-behaving applications presented as motivated future work pending in-vivo validation.

Headline correlation (delta_avg = 85.4%) excludes the bead that failed, hiding a ~17% per-source failure rate at the FoV edge: By restricting the headline statistic to the 5 most central beads and explicitly excluding bead #6 (which lay at the fiber-core edge), the reported delta_avg = 85.4% inflates apparent performance. For a method intended to record from an unknown distribution of neurons across the FoV (some inevitably peripheral), the relevant performance metric must include peripheral sources or report a separate radial-position-dependent failure rate. The paper does not quantify how delta_{g,n} depends on radial position d, nor what fraction of the FoV is reliably demixable - directly relevant since at-edge sources are the limiting case for any practical multi-cell recording.

Validation in a 50 um fixed brain slice with structural eGFP does not approximate the targeted in-vivo calcium-photometry regime: A fixed 50 um slice differs from a living brain in essentially every relevant way: no actual neuronal calcium dynamics (the 'activity' is still DMD-driven on a static structural label), no autofluorescence from blood and other tissue layers, only 50 um of tissue versus hundreds of micrometers above and below in vivo, no motion artifacts, and no out-of-focus background from neurons outside the slice plane. Furthermore, structural eGFP brightness produces high-contrast signals that bear little resemblance to a few-percent dF/F calcium indicator response convolved with the indicator kernel. Calling this 'mimicking more realistically' the in-vivo situation is an overstatement, and the implicit transfer of the 86.7% recovery to GCaMP-based recordings in living mice is unsupported.

Sample size in the brain-slice validation (N = 4 neurons, single slice, single mouse) cannot support a generalization claim: The validation rests on N=4 neurons in a single slice from a single GAD65-EGFP mouse. There is no second slice, no biological replicate, no varying neuron-density condition, and no scan over the number of simultaneously active sources. The reported delta_avg = 86.7% and the small sigma = 2.8% are based on a handful of pairwise correlations and have very low statistical power to distinguish among many alternative hypotheses (e.g., that performance degrades sharply with denser labeling, or with more strongly correlated sources). The validation should be either expanded or framed as preliminary.

GT-NMF testing uses only mildly correlated time traces (max ~31%), unlike real co-active neuronal populations: The maximum reported GT-GT temporal correlation is approximately 25-31%. Real neural calcium signals from functionally connected neurons - the very scientific use case for fiber photometry - can be far more correlated (>0.5-0.8 in some circuits). NMF identifiability degrades sharply as temporal correlations between sources increase. The paper validates the method only in a regime that is plausibly easier than its target application, yet the conclusions about 'single-source resolution' for neuronal activity are not bounded by this limitation.

MiniDART feasibility for multi-source photometry is asserted from a single-bead sensitivity test only: The paper concludes that the miniscope MiniDART can support full single-source-resolved fiber photometry in freely-behaving mice, but the actual experimental test is sensitivity to a single 10 um bead. The combined system has never been demonstrated end-to-end with multiple sources, NMF demixing, or the full proof-of-principle pipeline performed earlier on the sCMOS bench. The leap from 'CMOS detects a fingerprint with adequate SNR' to 'NMF demixing of dynamic multi-source recordings will work with this hardware' is unsupported; CMOS noise floor, bit-depth, gain non-linearity, and quantization may matter very differently when the algorithm must separate near-overlapping fingerprints with low-contrast intensity modulation.

Stability of fingerprints under fiber bending, temperature, and motion is never tested, despite being central to the calibration-free claim: The paper levels a strong criticism at TM-based approaches for needing SLM calibration that breaks under fiber bending, and uses this to motivate the proposed approach as 'calibration-free.' But unconstrained NMF demixing has its own analogous failure mode: it assumes that the spatial fingerprints remain temporally stable so they can be linearly separated. Any fiber bending, temperature change, or distal mechanical perturbation that alters the fingerprint during a recording will degrade NMF demixing, just as it would degrade TM-based imaging. The paper neither measures fingerprint drift over time nor reports robustness of NMF outputs to mechanical or thermal perturbation - precisely the experiments that would distinguish 'short MMF + NMF' from 'long MMF + SLM' on the dimension the paper itself emphasizes. This is the same standard the paper applies to others.

NMF rank selection and source-counting claim are unsupported; rank=9 for 6 sources can inflate apparent recovery: The proof-of-principle uses NMF rank = 9 for 6 actual beads (and bead #6 was not even recovered), and the brain-slice experiment uses rank = 5 for 4 neurons. Setting rank above the true source count gives the algorithm extra free components to absorb background and noise, which can artificially raise diagonal correlation values for the 'true' components. Yet the paper claims that 'counting unique NMF fingerprints' can identify the true source count - a claim that requires the rank-versus-source mapping to be reliable. The main text provides no validation: no false-positive/false-negative rate as a function of rank, no sweep over different ground-truth source counts, no replication in the brain-slice experiment, and the Discussion subtly walks the claim back ('possibly confirmed by a post-mortem evaluation'). Rank choice is the single most consequential user-facing parameter and is supported only by 'see supp info.'

The 'calibration-free' framing understates the practical burden of choosing rank in unknown samples: It is correct that no SLM-based wavefront calibration is required, but the user must still pick the NMF rank n_components, which the Methods concedes 'changes depending on the experiment.' In an unknown biological sample the true source count is unknown, and the paper itself states that higher-than-true rank produces 'replicas' of fingerprints and absorbs background. Calling the method 'calibration-free' understates this practical burden and its impact on result interpretation, especially because the source-counting claim depends on the same parameter. A more accurate framing would acknowledge that the method removes wavefront-calibration but introduces a model-selection problem.

Critical methods - the entire proof-of-principle setup, rank rationale, and supplementary analyses - are deferred to supp info: The proof-of-principle optical setup is the central apparatus that produces every quantitative result, yet its description is fully deferred to the supplementary information. Several other consequential items - rank-selection rationale, binning analysis, radial-dependence quantitative details, off-diagonal MAE table, and fingerprint shape ambiguity - are similarly deferred. A reader of the main text cannot evaluate (or reproduce) camera, magnification, exposure, frame rate, alignment tolerances, DMD pattern, or excitation power. Methodological transparency for headline numerical claims requires their experimental basis to be in the main body.

DMD time-trace shape, framerate, recording length, and noise model are not specified in the main text: Citation 57 (Chen et al. 2013, GCaMP6) and 43 (the authors' prior work) are invoked but the actual GT temporal profile (calcium-transient kernel? square pulses? sinusoids?), framerate, total recording length, photobleaching control, and shot/read-noise characterization are not stated in the main text. For the brain-slice experiment, the description 'literature-available time traces to mimic neuronal activity' is even vaguer - the reader cannot tell which calcium dataset, which event rates, or which dF/F amplitudes were used. Without these, neither the recovery numbers nor the difficulty of the task can be evaluated, and the experiments cannot be reproduced.

NMF hyperparameter choices are listed but not justified; sensitivity to initialization and seed is not reported: Setting alpha_W = alpha_H = 0 disables sparsity regularization, which the paper notes but does not motivate, even though incoherent fluorescence signals are 'naturally positive, linear, and sparse.' random_state = 0 fixes initialization, but NMF is non-convex and final factorization is known to depend on initialization. No robustness analysis (multiple seeds, alternative inits, range of max_iter) is reported. Given that the algorithm is the core contribution, sensitivity of delta_avg and zeta_avg to these choices is needed.

Self-imposed framerate standard (>=10 Hz) is not reported for the paper's own NMF recordings: The Discussion criticizes refs 53 and 54 for using a low (2 Hz) framerate as inadequate for calcium imaging and asserts that 'experiments are typically carried out with a framerate of at least 10 Hz.' But the actual NMF demixing experiments in Figs 2 and 3 do not state the framerate at which the sCMOS recorded the videos, the number of frames, the integration time, or the per-source signal-to-noise per frame. Holding others to a 10 Hz standard while not reporting one's own basis for comparison is an asymmetry; the paper should report its experimental framerate prominently in the main text.

Cross-talk metric zeta_avg ~= sigma_zeta indicates heavy variability that is not analyzed: A standard deviation (~7.29%) approximately equal to the mean (~7.06%) suggests heavy variability across off-diagonal coefficients - some pairs may exhibit large cross-talk while others are near zero. The paper does not break this distribution down (e.g., does cross-talk concentrate among GT-correlated source pairs like beads #3 and #4 with gamma_{3,4} = 31.2%?). For fiber photometry, the worst-case cross-talk between specific pairs - not the average - determines whether single-source resolution is justified, and this paired analysis is missing.

Miniscope vs sCMOS equivalence argument relies on pixel-binning which ignores detector-physics differences: Equating spatially binned sCMOS data to miniscope CMOS data ignores fundamental detector differences: pixel size, full-well capacity, read noise, quantum efficiency, dark current, bit depth, electronic gain non-linearity, and rolling-shutter artifacts. Binning a high-quality sCMOS image preserves photon SNR scaled by sqrt(N), but a CMOS detector with smaller wells and higher read noise per pixel can have qualitatively different noise. The 'visually indistinguishable' binning comparison therefore does not establish that the miniscope is sufficient for the demixing task - especially in low-contrast regimes that calcium imaging requires.

No quantitative SNR or noise-floor measurement for the miniscope; the system saturates at the lowest practical settings: Saturation at the lowest practical settings for d < 20 um with a 10 um bead implies the dynamic range available for actual neurons (which are typically dimmer per pixel and lower contrast in vivo) may be much smaller than for this test source. The paper does not report SNR, dF/F sensitivity, dark current, read noise, or quantization step in absolute units.
