Without these, the claim that 'the miniscope is sensitive enough' cannot be evaluated for realistic regimes - calcium dF/F of a few percent against autofluorescence-dominated background is the actual demand.

Discussion concedes CNMF is superior for calcium signals, undermining the unconstrained-NMF baseline as evidence for in-vivo viability: The authors acknowledge that constrained NMF (CNMF) outperforms unconstrained NMF for calcium signals but choose unconstrained NMF for proof-of-principle. This is reasonable as a baseline demonstration, but creates an asymmetry: the recovery numbers (~85%) are presented as positive evidence for the method's viability while the same authors acknowledge a known-better alternative. The paper would either need a CNMF comparison on the same data or a clearer statement that the unconstrained-NMF numbers are a lower bound that may not transfer to the actual targeted regime (calcium dynamics in vivo).

Comparison with prior learning-based MMF approaches is qualitative and one-sided: The Discussion dismisses learning-based approaches (refs 53, 54) by arguing they are dataset-specific, but does not perform a controlled comparison on equivalent data nor reproduce those methods. Moreover, NMF itself depends on the assumption that fingerprints are stable and independent enough to be linearly demixed - an assumption that, like a training set, is fiber- and condition-specific. Framing the proposed method as more 'general' is asserted, not demonstrated, and the paper would benefit from at least a qualitative head-to-head on the same MMF/sample.

Threshold separating short-fiber 'fingerprints' from long-fiber speckles is never quantitatively defined: The paper repeatedly contrasts 'scattering fingerprints' (their regime) with 'fully developed speckles' (long-fiber regime), and the entire premise that NMF can demix without TM calibration depends on this distinction. Yet no quantitative criterion is offered for when this transition occurs as a function of MMF length, NA, core diameter, wavelength, or number of guided modes. The paper cites Okamoto (ref 56) generally but does not present a relevant length scale (mode-mixing length, equilibrium length). A reader using a different MMF cannot determine whether their fiber will produce 'fingerprints' amenable to unconstrained NMF.

Long-MMF generalization claim is invoked from prior work but not demonstrated in this paper: The paper is about short MMFs and explicitly distinguishes the short-fiber 'fingerprint' regime from the long-fiber 'fully developed speckle' regime. Asserting that the unconstrained NMF method 'is also readily applied for long MMF applications' invokes the prior work for support but does not show that long MMFs in the present setup yield equivalent results. Given the well-known sensitivity of long-fiber speckles to bending and temperature - which the paper itself emphasizes - this generalization should be presented as a hypothesis, not a fact.

Fiber length used in experiments is never explicitly stated; reader must infer it: Fiber length appears as '< 10 mm' (Introduction, Conclusion), '~ 8 mm long' (Figure 1 caption), and the Methods describes '2 mm of it sticking out of the ferrule' from a 6 mm ferrule, suggesting around 8 mm total. The Methods section never states an exact fiber length used in the experiments, despite this being a critical parameter that determines whether the fiber operates in the 'fingerprint' regime that the entire claim depends on.

Radial-position-encoded ring diameter rho(d) is presented as a localization tool without calibration or replication: The relationship rho(d) is presented as monotonic and useful for inferring source localization, but no calibration curve, fit to a waveguide model, or uncertainty quantification is provided. The paper does not state how many sweeps were performed, the number of repeats, whether the relationship is preserved across different fibers, or how bending alters rho(d). As stated, it is a qualitative observation used to motivate a localization claim that has not been quantitatively demonstrated.

Hedged statement that fingerprints are 'not ambiguous' with source position ignores azimuthal degeneracy: The radial sweep in Fig 4 only varies one azimuthal angle (the 'diagonal white dashed line') and the paper itself notes that this angle 'always coincides with the alignment angle of the 2 central bright points of the fingerprint patterns.' Two sources at the same radius but different azimuthal angles would presumably yield rotated versions of the same fingerprint, so the rho(d) information alone is not sufficient to localize a source uniquely. The phrasing 'seem to not be ambiguous' is hedged and not justified by data on multiple azimuths or by combinations at the same radius. This affects the source-counting and identifiability claims downstream.

Off-diagonal MAE formula has an inconsistent normalization factor: For a symmetric correlation matrix with N_s sources, the number of unique off-diagonal pairs is N_s(N_s - 1)/2 and the number of off-diagonal entries (counting both (i,j) and (j,i)) is N_s(N_s - 1). The denominator 1/[2(N_s - 1)] does not correspond to either; it would only match a particular case (N_s = 2 or one specific symmetry assumption). The upper limit of the sum is shown as N_s - 1 rather than N_s. As written, this expression does not correctly compute a mean for arbitrary N_s and should be revisited.

Headline 'comparable to FNO/MGNO/LNO/GNO' claim is supported by training loss, not test loss: The single head-to-head comparison in the paper (Fig. 2c) plots training loss across models. Training loss is dominated by capacity, optimizer, and number of epochs and is not a meaningful cross-model accuracy metric — the standard FNO benchmark protocol from [24] reports relative L2 test error on a held-out set. The Methods section also describes the training procedure only for ONE; it never specifies how the FCN/PCANN/RBM/GNO/LNO/MGNO/FNO baselines were re-trained, on what splits, or to what optimum. Combined with the inconsistency that other PDEs in the paper plot validation loss (Figs. 2f, 3c, 3d, 4b) while only Darcy uses training loss, this undermines the central 'comparable performance' claim. Without test/validation numbers and matched baseline protocols the comparison is not interpretable.

Experimental demonstration covers only a single DONN diffraction stage on Darcy — abstract's 'experimentally demonstrate' is overstated: The abstract claims 'we numerically and experimentally demonstrate the capability of the ONE architecture' across five PDEs. The actual experimental measurement is the output of one DONN kernel of one branch, on Darcy data — not a full DONN, not the cascaded 4x (real-space + Fourier-space + nonlinearity) blocks, no end-to-end PDE prediction, and zero experimental work for magnetostatic, Navier-Stokes, Maxwell, or multiphysics PDEs. All headline accuracy results came from PyTorch simulation on an Nvidia RTX 6000 GPU. The claim 'experimentally validating the feasibility of the ONE architecture in solving PDEs' is a substantial leap from a single optical diffraction stage to end-to-end PDE solving on optical hardware.

Throughput claim of >1e5 acceleration relies on hypothetical >1000 Hz SLMs — actual hardware is 60 Hz: The demonstrated DONN setup uses HOLOEYE LC 2012 SLMs at 60 Hz refresh and a Thorlabs CS165MU1 camera at 34.8 fps — at minimum ~17 ms per instance, before counting the four cascaded blocks. The >1e5 speedup is computed by substituting hypothetical >1000 Hz SLMs/cameras and comparing to an unspecified 'minutes to hours' classical solver baseline. No per-PDE solver, hardware, resolution, or accuracy target is specified for the comparison. The 5 ms FNO inference time used as the 'state-of-the-art ML' comparator is also taken from [24] without matching configuration. Net effect: a projected-hardware-vs-arbitrary-solver number is presented as an achieved speedup. The actual demonstrated system has not been measured for inference latency anywhere in the paper.

1e7 power-advantage claim ignores laser, ADC/DAC, photodetector amplifiers, electronic nonlinearity, and full inference dynamic energy: The 10 uW per-SLM number is the leakage current of liquid-crystal cells alone — i.e., static idle power for one SLM. It excludes (i) the laser source power (CPS532 diodes are typically hundreds of mW), (ii) every analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog conversion at the input encoder and camera readout, (iii) photodetector amplifier power, (iv) the electronic processing and O/E/O conversion required between every one of the four cascaded blocks for the nonlinearity, (v) the GPU/CPU executing the nonlinearity and physics-parameter branch, and (vi) the SLM driver electronics and FPGAs that load each frame. A true energy-per-inference number for ONE is never computed. Comparing one component's idle leakage to a GPU's total inference power yields a 7-order-of-magnitude advantage that is not a like-for-like comparison.

Maxwell's-equations claim is supported only by single-component (E_x) auto-regressive prediction with an internally inconsistent time window: Two compounding problems undermine the Maxwell demonstration. First, the network is trained only on E_x — one of six coupled Maxwell field components (E_x, E_y, E_z, H_x, H_y, H_z) — so the divergence/curl coupling that defines Maxwell's equations is never enforced in training. The abstract and Results frame this as 'solving Maxwell's equations', which is a substantial overstatement of single-component time-series prediction in a periodic dielectric metasurface. Second, the time window 'between 300000 fs to 160000 fs' has a start later than its end, and 'backward fed' is not defined; the reader cannot determine whether the network is forward or time-reversed propagating, nor where the predicted 40000 fs window starts. Together these make the Maxwell result both narrower than claimed and not reproducible.

'Multiphysics' demonstration is single-time-step regression from one physics field, not coupled-PDE solving: The Multiphysics PDEs section frames the task as solving the coupled electric-current and heat-transfer PDEs and is invoked in the abstract as 'coupled PDEs in a multiphysics system'. But (i) the network input is only the electric current layer (one physics field), not both V(x,y,t) and T(x,y,t), and (ii) the network output is the temperature at a single fixed time step (t=55 s), not a time-evolving solution. The result is a static, single-snapshot regression rather than a coupled time-dependent PDE solve; no validation is performed at other t_n, with other pulse shapes, or with the coupling residual. The claim that ONE solves multiphysics PDEs is therefore weaker than presented.

Optical end-to-end implementability is overclaimed — channel mixing, four cascaded blocks, and electronic nonlinearity require unmeasured O/E/O conversions: The architecture has four cascaded (Fourier + real + nonlinear) blocks. Because the nonlinearity is electronic, every block boundary requires opto-electronic conversion, electronic processing, and re-encoding onto the next SLM. These conversions have latency, energy, ADC noise, and bit-precision constraints that dominate real photonic accelerators and are entirely omitted from both the throughput and energy claims. Separately, the channel-mixing operation between DONN kernels is referenced only by citing [24] (FNO uses 1x1 channel convolutions) and is never specified in optical-hardware terms — the number of channels, encoding scheme, and SLM/photodetector mapping are not given. Both gaps mean the 'all-optical except nonlinearity' claim is materially incomplete.

Hardware-noise robustness is shown only in simulation — no measured noise from the actual XBAR pipeline: The noise study (Fig. 5c-d) injects zero-mean i.i.d. Gaussian noise on simulated MVM outputs. Real photonic XBARs produce noise that is signal-dependent (shot noise scales as sqrt(I)), correlated across detector elements, and includes thermal/Johnson noise at the transimpedance amplifier — all unmodeled here. The claim 'the noise influence ... is not substantial' rests on transferring the noise floor of a *prior, separate* calibrated XBAR [36] onto the present ONE result; the present optical XBAR was not built. Furthermore, the Discussion concedes that 'noise-aware training can be incorporated to mitigate the discrepancy between models and practical systems', acknowledging that the present results were not obtained with such mitigations. The robustness conclusion is therefore a projection, not a measurement.

No baselines for Navier-Stokes, Maxwell, magnetostatic, or multiphysics — selective comparison: The Darcy section contains an explicit Fig. 2c head-to-head against FCN/PCANN/RBM/GNO/LNO/MGNO/FNO. The other four PDE sections (magnetostatic, Navier-Stokes, Maxwell, multiphysics) show only ONE's own validation curves with no baseline. The Navier-Stokes dataset is reused from FNO [24], so an FNO baseline is straightforward; its absence — coupled with the inclusion of baselines only on Darcy where the curves overlap — gives the appearance of selective reporting. The reader cannot evaluate the 'comparable to state-of-the-art ML' claim for any PDE besides Darcy.

Encoder grey-level mapping formula contains the input-data symbol only on the LHS — formula as stated cannot encode the input: As written, the right-hand side has no dependence on d, so every input value would be assigned the same grey level. The intended formula is presumably d_grey = int( (d - d_min) * (255 - 130) / (d_max - d_min) + 130 ), i.e., a missing (d - d_min) factor. Since this formula governs how all input 2D data are loaded onto SLM0 in the experimental Darcy demonstration, the methods description is incorrect, and a reader cannot reproduce the encoding without guessing the correct expression.

Spatial-light-modulation equation drops the imaginary unit from the phase factor: The transmission coefficient is defined two equations earlier as t(x,y,S) e^{i*phi(x,y,S)}. In this final modulation equation the i is missing — the exponent reads e^{phi(x,y,S)}, which is a real-valued amplitude factor rather than the intended complex phase modulation. Either a typo or a notational inconsistency, but as stated the equation does not describe phase modulation.

DONN model is described as both 'phase-only' and 'coupled' simultaneously — which simulation produced the figures is unclear: The Methods description is internally contradictory: 'phase-only spatial light modulation in [0, 2pi]' and 'coupled spatial light modulation' are different physical models. The Gumbel-softmax training was specifically introduced because real SLM amplitude/phase response is discrete and coupled. It is not stated whether Figs. 2-4 (the headline accuracy results) used the idealized phase-only model or the coupled discrete-table model. If they used the idealized model, the comparison to FNO is on a network that cannot be physically realized; if they used the coupled model, no measurement has been made of the gap between the two.

Branch-combination operator (sum + product) and broadcasting rule for the physics-parameter branch are under-specified: The text says F(u) and R(u) are added and the physics-parameter branch output T(d) is 'multiplied and merged onto two other branches to have the final output g(x,y,t)'. It is not specified whether T(d) multiplies F(u)+R(u) or each branch separately, whether the multiplication is element-wise, broadcast across spatial coordinates, or a tensor product. Because T(d) encodes pulse height/width (scalars in time only), the broadcasting rule materially determines the model's expressivity in the multiphysics task. The reader cannot reproduce the network from this prose.

Architecture size (channels, layers per block, parameter count) is never reported: Four cascaded blocks is the only architecture-scale hyperparameter mentioned. The Methods report learning rates and epoch counts but never report channel widths, number of DONN layers per block, MVM matrix sizes, or total parameter count. The comparison in Fig. 2c against FNO/MGNO/etc. therefore has no parameter-budget axis: the reader cannot tell whether ONE matches FNO with similar or vastly different parameter counts. This is essential for any 'comparable performance' claim.

Darcy permeability is binary {3, 12} — likely simpler than the standard FNO Gaussian-random-field benchmark: The standard Darcy benchmark in [24] uses a continuous log-Gaussian-random-field permeability, which is significantly harder than a binary {3, 12} field. The Methods cite [24] for the dataset but the prose describes a binary k(x,y). If the Fig. 2c baselines (GNO, LNO, MGNO, FNO) report their numbers on the continuous-field version while ONE reports on the binary version, the comparison is not on equal footing. The paper does not clarify which version of the dataset is used, and the binary case is uncharacteristically simple for this benchmark family.

Magnetostatic dataset spans only 8 bias-field samples — generalization claim rests on a tiny manifold: The magnetostatic Poisson training distribution is generated from only 8 bias-field directions at a fixed magnitude, evolved for 1 ns. The resulting (M, H) pairs lie on a low-dimensional manifold determined by these 8 starting conditions, and the network can effectively memorize the trajectories. Since the magnetostatic Poisson equation is linear and has a closed-form Green's-function solution, 'good performance' on this narrow distribution is weak evidence that ONE has learned the operator. The paper does not report performance on unseen bias directions or magnitudes.

Magnetostatic learning rate of 1.0 for DONN parameters is unusually high and unexplained: Adam learning rates of 1.0 are more than two orders of magnitude higher than typical (1e-3 to 1e-4) and would normally cause divergence. The other PDE tasks in the paper use 0.1 for DONN parameters. The paper offers no explanation for why magnetostatic uses 1.0; it is plausibly a typo, but if intentional it suggests the DONN parameterization is unusual (e.g., a Gumbel-softmax temperature). Lacking the rationale, this hyperparameter is not reproducible.

Maxwell metasurface dataset (1200 samples from a ~195k-point 4-parameter grid) gives sparse coverage with no test-distance analysis: Each Lumerical FDTD simulation is parameterized by four pillar radii in [39.5, 44.5] um with step 0.25 um, giving 21^4 = 194,481 possible configurations. With 1200 random samples (~0.6% coverage), the validation set's 200 designs may be near-neighbors of training designs. Without an analysis of how validation accuracy depends on parameter-space distance from training, 'good performance' may reflect interpolation between near-identical metasurfaces rather than learning of the underlying operator.

Navier-Stokes 10-step rollout (1 ms at dt=1e-4 s) is short relative to the FNO benchmark and the eddy turnover time: 10 timesteps at dt=1e-4 s is a 1 ms horizon — orders of magnitude shorter than the eddy turnover time of viscous turbulent flow at v=1e-3, and short relative to standard FNO Navier-Stokes benchmarks (e.g., t=1 to t=20 in [24]). No rollout-error growth analysis is shown. Reporting this as 'solving the Navier-Stokes equation' overstates the demonstration; it is a short-horizon vorticity prediction, not a time-integration solver.

Quantitative loss/error numbers are absent — comparisons rely entirely on overlapping curves: No numerical accuracy or loss value is stated for any model on any task anywhere in the paper. 'Comparable to FNO/GNO/MGNO/LNO' is supported only by visually overlapping curves on a log-scale plot, with no error bars and no stated test-error number. This is well below the norm of the neural-operator literature this paper claims to compete with, and prevents future work from benchmarking against the present results.

Error metric is inconsistent across PDE tasks — absolute, relative, normalized-by-max — without justification: Across the five PDE tasks the metric varies: 'training loss' (Darcy), 'validation loss' (others), pixelwise 'absolute error' and 'relative error' (Darcy, Navier-Stokes, Maxwell, multiphysics), and 'normalized error with respect to maximum field strength in the ground truth' (magnetostatic). These metrics are not interchangeable — max-normalization can hide large fractional errors in low-magnitude regions. A reader cannot compare ONE's accuracy across tasks, nor verify the 'comparable performance' claim per PDE.

Speckle and alignment errors are acknowledged but the offered mitigations (in-loop hardware training, adaptive realignment) are not performed: Two key sources of model-vs-experiment error are explicitly identified — speckle from high-order diffraction interference and alignment sensitivity to external variations — and in both cases the proposed mitigations (in-loop hardware training, adaptive pixel-by-pixel re-alignment) are referenced from prior works but not performed in this work. For a regression-based PDE solver, even small field-level errors can dominate the final output. The text concedes that errors are present 'for performing regression tasks' but provides no quantitative error budget or measured end-to-end Darcy prediction loss on the optical setup.

Sign information cannot be encoded by [130, 255] amplitude grey-level mapping — relevant for time-dependent PDE inputs: SLM grey levels [130, 255] modulate the amplitude of light, which is non-negative. Mapping a signed input (e.g., vorticity, electric field, magnetization components) into a non-negative amplitude makes the sign recoverable only through spatial context, not directly. The Darcy permeability is non-negative, so this is not an issue there, but the prose explicitly says input data 'span both negative and positive values' and the architecture is later applied to vorticity, E_x, and M components. The encoder's inability to represent sign is a structural limitation of the experimental setup that is not flagged.

Discussion is ~3 sentences and omits major limitations evident in the body: The Discussion only identifies positive future work (active learning, noise-aware training, regression beyond PDEs). It does not acknowledge: only Darcy was partially experimentally validated; Maxwell training only learns one of six field components; Navier-Stokes is a 10-step rollout; multiphysics is single-snapshot regression; the encoder cannot represent sign directly; throughput and energy claims are projections; channel mixing is not specified for optical hardware. A standard limitations paragraph in this domain would acknowledge most of these.

Confidence weighting formula gives the most-confident network the smallest weight: For confidence c in [0.5, 1] (since c = mean(|P_i - 0.5| + 0.5)), each numerator (1-c_k) is in [0, 0.5] and the denominator is just the L1 norm of those numerators, putting the ratio in [0, 1] and exp(.) in [1, e]. Crucially, *higher* confidence c_k yields a *smaller* numerator and a *smaller* w_k, i.e. the most confident sub-network is given the *least* weight. This is the opposite of what the prose advertises ('grading module ... allowing adaptive memory fusing to produce an optimized prediction'). Either the formula has a sign/inversion error or the prose mis-describes the algorithm. As written, the ablation result in Fig. 3 cannot be explained by Eq. (4).

'Confidence' definition collapses to a constant if predictions are binarized as stated: The Methods explicitly state that P_i 'is binarized to be either 0 or 1' in Eq. (3). Under that statement |P_i - 0.5| is identically 0.5 for every pixel, so c is identically 1.0 for every sub-network and Eq. (3) provides no discriminative information. All weights from Eq. (4) would then be equal and the 'confidence-based ensemble' would degenerate to a uniform average. If P_i is intended to be the pre-binarization sigmoid output in [0,1], that contradicts the explicit binarization clause. The reader cannot determine which is correct, and either reading is incompatible with the architecture being claimed.

'Forgetting mechanism' for S1/S2 is the central novelty but is under-specified: The 'memory wiping' distinguishes S1/S2 from L3 and underlies the multi-scale claim, but the paper never specifies what wiping means in implementation terms (re-initialize weights? from what distribution? reset only optimizer state? reload a checkpoint?), nor at what cadence each of S1 vs S2 wipes (the word 'alternatively' is repeated without disambiguation). The Methods sections 'Multi-scale memory dynamic-learning network', 'Neural network architecture', and 'Confidence-based ensemble algorithm' do not address these. Without this information the architectural mechanism that supposedly drives the headline accuracy gain cannot be reproduced.

Network architecture is too under-specified for reproduction or capacity comparison: Three conv layers plus one FC layer is described without channel counts, kernel sizes, strides, dropout probability, or batch-norm batch size (which is non-trivial under online training with 500-frame windows). This prevents reproduction. It also matters for the central baseline comparison: MMDN aggregates 3 sub-networks (~3x StaticNN parameters), so the 'two-orders' improvement may partly reflect ensemble capacity rather than dynamic adaptation. A capacity-matched comparison (e.g., 3x-wider StaticNN, or 3 independent StaticNNs ensembled with the same weights but no online updates) is missing.

StaticNN baseline is weak and not parameter- or training-matched: The headline 'two orders of magnitude improvement' compares MMDN to a single network trained on the first 500 s and then frozen. Anyone deploying a learning-based MMF reconstructor under known channel drift would at minimum periodically retrain or fine-tune. The paper compares against neither (a) periodic offline retraining, (b) supervised online fine-tuning on actual labeled batches, nor (c) any prior dynamic method cited in the Introduction. In addition, the initial paired-data sizes are not stated to be matched (StaticNN appears to see ~50,000 frames; MMDN '20,000 paired data' for the natural-image experiment), so the comparison conflates dynamic-learning benefit with capacity and data-size differences.

'Arbitrary optical fields' overstates what the amplitude-only setup demonstrates: The Abstract claims transmission of 'arbitrary optical fields', but the experimental section uses a 'binary SLM as the amplitude modulator' on an 'amplitude-to-amplitude optical setup', reconstructing binarized 0/1 patterns. There is no transmission of phase, polarization, or grayscale amplitude. In MMF imaging, 'arbitrary optical fields' typically connotes complex amplitude or full-Stokes transmission. The claim should be tightened (e.g., to 'arbitrary binary amplitude patterns'), otherwise it materially overstates the demonstrated capability.

'1024 spatial degrees of freedom' equates SLM pixels with optical modes: 1024 = 32x32 is the SLM input pixel count, not the number of independent optical modes successfully transmitted. The proper figure of merit for MMF channel capacity is the number of supported propagation modes, which depends on V-number and is generally not equal to SLM pixel count. The paper does not measure distinguishable independent modes through the channel and does not even compute the V-number for the 200 um MMFs at 561 nm. The Methods section acknowledges this distinction obliquely ('it is theoretically possible to input images of larger pixel resolution'), but the abstract framing remains capacity-flavored when the result is image-recovery on a 1024-pixel input.

Per-pixel accuracy is reported as the headline number where per-image accuracy is what matters: All headline figures (99.97%, '< 0.1% error rate', 'two orders improved') are per-pixel binary classification accuracies. For 1024-pixel patterns at 99.97% per-pixel accuracy, the expected per-image error count is ~0.3 pixels, so a substantial fraction of images contain at least one wrong pixel. Yet the video section itself shows that even ~2% per-pixel error rate destroys decoded quality. Reporting per-pixel accuracy as the headline is misleading about how reliable the channel actually is for downstream applications. A per-image accuracy or bit-error-rate would be more informative and would be lower than the cited number.

Self-supervised pseudo-label training validated only over 1000 s with no error-accumulation analysis: The authors explicitly recognize that pseudo-label drift can accumulate, then claim the multi-scale architecture controls it - but provide no quantitative analysis of error accumulation, no controlled experiment with intermittently injected true labels, and no theoretical bound. The reported 1000 s (~17 min) duration shows no degradation, but this is an order of magnitude shorter than the 'long-term' framing suggests for practical deployment (multi-hour, multi-day). Without a longer time series or a stress-test on a deliberately destabilized channel, the central 'long-term' claim is supported only out to 1000 s.

5 s update interval is a critical hyperparameter with no sensitivity analysis: The 5 s interval is justified post-hoc as 'half' of an asserted 10 s stability window. The paper provides no ablation across update intervals (1 s / 2 s / 5 s / 10 s / 20 s) and does not characterize how sensitive the headline accuracy is to this choice. Since update frequency directly trades off compute cost against tracking speed, and the central novelty is the dynamic update itself, this is the most important hyperparameter to sweep and it is not swept.

Ensemble ablation confounds fiber length, fiber type, and pattern resolution: The Fig. 3 ablation compares S1, S2, L3, and the ensemble across two cases that differ on three axes simultaneously - fiber length (100 m vs 1 km), refractive-index profile (GI vs SI), and resolution (16x16 vs 32x32). The flipped relative ordering of L3 vs S1/S2 between the two cases ('long-term works better most of the time' on SI-200; opposite on GI-200) cannot be attributed to channel volatility alone. A 2x2 design (length x resolution) on the same fiber type would be needed to support claims about which memory scale matters when.

'10x' ensemble improvement is reported without confidence intervals or replication: A 10-fold improvement at the >99% regime is error-rate reduction from ~10^-2 to ~10^-3, which is highly sensitive to the exact denominator and to single-trial fluctuations. The paper reports a single 1000 s run per condition, with no error bars, no replication across fibers or days, and no statistical test. Given the authors' own emphasis on day-to-day fiber drift and jitter, a single-run ratio is insufficient to validate the claim.

No ablation against supervised online updates or against simpler S1+L3 architecture: Two control experiments are missing. (1) An oracle that performs the same online updates with *true* labels would establish how much accuracy is lost to self-supervision specifically; this is the natural upper bound and it is not measured. (2) An S1+L3 (or S2+L3) ablation removing one short-term subnetwork would show whether two short-term experts are necessary or whether one suffices. The paper claims 'two short-term + one long-term' as a design but provides no evidence supporting two over one.

Train/evaluate workflow within a 5 s batch is not clearly described: Within each 5 s batch, MMDN appears to (a) infer pseudo-labels on the batch frames, (b) train on those pseudo-labels, and (c) report accuracy against the known input patterns - but it is unclear whether reported accuracy is on the same frames used for training (overfit to batch) or on a held-out range, and whether 'pseudo-label' means MMDN's most recent inference or a re-inference after training. This methodological detail directly affects whether the reported accuracies reflect generalization or over-fitting to the training batch.

'700-fold throughput enhancement' has no main-text derivation and may simply restate the H.264 ratio: This is a headline contribution, also abstracted as 'orders of throughput enhancement', but the main text gives no formula, no per-pixel bit budget, and no comparison condition - the entire quantitative claim is delegated to a supplementary figure. The cited compression ratio is 1.39 per-mille (~720x), which is a property of H.264 alone and independent of MMDN. The reader cannot determine whether '700-fold' is a genuine gain attributable to MMDN's high-fidelity transmission or simply the codec compression ratio.

Bandwidth budget for real-time video is asserted, not demonstrated: Doing the arithmetic from the paper's own numbers: 480x480x24 bits x 20 fps x 1.39e-3 ~ 1.54e5 bits/s, while a 32x32 binary pattern at 150 fps yields exactly 1.54e5 bits/s. This leaves zero margin for retransmission, FEC, or update overhead. The claim of 'adequate bandwidth for real-time transmission' should be supported with the explicit budget rather than asserted.

StaticNN-vs-MMDN video gap may be an FEC artifact, not an MMDN advantage: The argument that '<2% bit error collapses video quality' motivates MMDN, but raw H.264 with no FEC is famously fragile to bit errors. A practical encoded-video system would use forward error correction, channel coding, or interleaving, none of which are considered. If a standard FEC layer were applied to both StaticNN and MMDN outputs the gap would likely shrink substantially, so the dramatic StaticNN failure is at least as much a codec-choice artifact as a MMDN-vs-StaticNN comparison.

Figure reference in video-decoding paragraph points to the wrong figure: This sentence is in the 'Long-term high-throughput video transmission' section, which corresponds to Fig. 5. Fig. 4 (b) is the Fashion-MNIST scalability panel and contains nothing about a 160-180 s asterisk. The intended reference is Fig. 5 (b). As written, the figure pointer is broken and disrupts a reader trying to verify the non-recoverability claim.

Headline accuracy figures are scattered and not systematically reported: Different sections cite >99.9% (Abstract), 99.97% and '< 0.1% error rate' (Long-term spatial transmission, 1km), 'error rate to 2e-6' (100 m case), and SSIM > 0.995 (video). There is no consolidated table mapping each (fiber length, resolution, dataset) configuration to its headline number with denominators stated; some numbers appear to be averages over time and others over space, but this is left implicit. A reader trying to verify the abstract's '>99.9% / 1024 DoF / 1km' claim must cross-reference figures.

Hellinger distance formula has unusual normalization and a likely index typo: The standard Hellinger-squared distance is H^2(P,Q) = (1/2) sum_{i=1}^{n} (sqrt(p_i) - sqrt(q_i))^2 with P and Q normalized so that sum_i p_i = sum_i q_i = 1, giving values in [0,1]. The paper sums from i=0 (n+1 terms) and treats P, Q as 'speckle energy distributions' from raw summed speckle images without describing normalization. If P and Q are not normalized to 1, equation (2) is not Hellinger distance and produced numbers are not comparable to typical Hellinger ranges. Combined with the lower-index typo this is a real concern about what was actually computed for the channel-stability metric.

Generalization claim rests on a single intra-domain transfer between similar handwriting datasets: The 'generalization' result is one transfer between two close subsets of the same family (Latin letters to digits, both 32x32 binarized handwriting). The conclusion that the network 'has good generalization performance' is broad relative to that single positive case. No transfer to substantially different distributions (natural scenes, grayscale, non-handwriting), no negative case, and no quantification of transfer breadth is shown.

Headline 'six-fold' improvement is a simulated, optimization-metric-derived ratio, not an experimental measurement: The 0.045 vs 0.0075 wavelength-averaged Strehl ratios that produce the '6x' headline are reported only from simulations in Section 2.2 ('In our simulations, the optimized broadband meta-optics displayed significantly larger wavelength-averaged Strehl Ratios'). The PSF characterization (Sec 4.3) measures the fabricated lens but the paper does not report measured Strehl values from the PSFs in the main text. Compounding this, the figure of merit being optimized (log-product of modified Strehl ratios) is essentially the same quantity as the evaluation metric, so the ratio in part reflects 'we trained on this metric, the baseline did not.' The abstract should either present measured Strehl numbers, or describe the 6x as a simulation prediction; and the comparison should be supplemented with a metric the meta-optic was not directly trained for (e.g., PSNR with a fixed reconstruction pipeline).

Aperture and periodicity in Methods 4.2 contradict main text and Fig. 1 caption: Section 4.2 states a 10 cm aperture and 10 µm periodicity with 2500x2500 atoms, but 2500*10 µm = 2.5 cm, so the sentence is internally inconsistent. The Introduction, Section 2.2, and Discussion all state a 1 cm aperture (~1000 lambda), and Fig. 1 caption gives Lambda = 4 µm. Only diameter = 1 cm and periodicity = 4 µm produce 2500x2500 atoms self-consistently. As written, Methods 4.2 misdescribes the simulated/fabricated lens, and a careful reader cannot tell which of the figures was the actual lens analyzed. This needs a corrigendum.

Number of optimization wavelengths reported as 8 in Section 2.2 and 13 in Section 4.2: Section 2.2 reports 8 optimized wavelengths 'due to memory constraints', but Methods 4.2 says 'During optimization, a total of 13 samples of wavelengths are used uniformly spanning from 8 µm to 12 µm.' These cannot both describe the same simulation. The wavelength sampling density directly determines how representative the FoM is of the continuous 8-12 µm band, and underlies the claim about non-sampled wavelengths still outperforming the hyperboloid. The two numbers should be reconciled, or a clear distinction made between training and evaluation samples.

FoM = log(prod S_i) does not actually 'constrain uniform performance' as claimed: log(prod S_i) is monotone in each S_i and does not by itself enforce equality of S_i. The argument that 'FoM is maximized when all S_i are identical' holds only with a fixed-sum (or fixed-mean) constraint on the S_i, which the optimization does not impose. The objective primarily strongly penalizes any S_i approaching zero (since log -> -infinity), which empirically suppresses worst-case wavelengths but is not a uniformity constraint. Separately, this FoM is unbounded below as any one S_i -> 0, which is a relevant numerical caveat. The justification should be tightened (e.g., compared empirically to alternative FoMs like the arithmetic mean or min-Strehl) rather than asserted.

'Modified Strehl ratio' departs from textbook definition and lacks specified frequency cutoffs: The 'modified Strehl ratio' is defined as the integral of the normalized MTF over a finite frequency window (kx1, ky1), but: (a) the conventional Strehl ratio is a peak-PSF intensity ratio, not an MTF integral, so reusing the name is confusing; (b) the cutoff frequencies kx1, ky1 are introduced symbolically but never assigned numerical values, and the absolute Strehl numbers (0.045, 0.018, 0.0075) and the 6x ratio depend on this choice. Different cutoffs would change the numbers and could change the ranking. The paper should either rename the quantity (e.g., 'frequency-bounded MTF volume') or specify the cutoffs and their relationship to the diffraction-limited cutoff, so that absolute numbers can be interpreted and reproduced.

MTF defined as the modulus of the FT of intensity, not normalized to OTF(0,0): The conventional MTF is |OTF| / |OTF(0,0)|, i.e. normalized so that M(0,0) = 1. As written, M(0,0) is the integrated PSF intensity, which depends on lens transmission and not just imaging quality. The paper does subsequently normalize by the diffraction-limited MTF (M-hat = M / D), but dividing two un-normalized magnitudes only equals dividing two normalized MTFs if their DC values are equal -- which would only hold under specific transmission conditions. Either the MTF definition should be written with the conventional normalization, or the paper should justify why the un-normalized form is equivalent here.

DNN surrogate accuracy is never validated against held-out RCWA simulations: The DNN surrogate is the differentiable bridge from geometry to phase that drives gradient descent over 2500x2500 meta-atom parameters. Yet the paper reports no held-out test loss, no comparison of DNN-predicted vs. RCWA-simulated transmission, no analysis of error in regions of parameter space far from training samples. The optimizer can readily drive p toward configurations the DNN extrapolates incorrectly, in which case the realized fabrication does not match the simulation. Because the simple-vs-complex comparison also has very different surrogate training-data sizes (101k vs 6.464M samples), the difference between simple and complex performance may also partly reflect surrogate quality differences rather than only library expressiveness. Quantitative surrogate validation is needed.

Polarization insensitivity claimed structurally but never measured: The Abstract, Introduction, and Section 2.2 all advertise polarization insensitivity, but it is asserted only from meta-atom symmetry; no PSF or imaging measurement under TE vs. TM polarized illumination is reported. Four-fold symmetry of an idealized isolated meta-atom does not guarantee polarization-insensitive performance for the assembled lens, especially under oblique incidence (the optimization includes 10 deg) and in the presence of fabrication asymmetries from DRIE sidewall angles or alignment. This is a verifiable claim that should be backed up with a polarization-resolved measurement.

Quantitative comparison with the refractive lens baseline is missing: The Introduction motivates the work by noting that prior meta-optics have lower image quality than refractive lenses. Fig. 4 shows side-by-side outputs of refractive, hyperboloid, and MTF-engineered optics 'in the wild', but no quantitative metric (PSNR, MTF50, line-pair resolution) is reported for any of them. The natural strength claim is 'closes the gap with refractive optics', and a number is needed to support it. As presented the reader cannot tell whether the meta-optic is 90% or 30% as good as the refractive lens. The headline 6x claim is against a strawman hyperboloid, not the refractive lens that motivates the paper.

Quantitative imaging metric (PSNR) values relegated to supplement; reference image and alignment unspecified: The only quantitative experimental imaging metric is PSNR, but the actual numbers and the procedure used to compute them (reference image, alignment/registration, masking, whether reconstruction is included) are not in the main text. PSNR values for natural-looking targets depend strongly on the reference choice, and the meta-optic vs. hyperboloid comparison can flip depending on whether deconvolution is applied symmetrically (see related fairness comment). Headline numbers and a precise PSNR-computation protocol should be in the main text.

Semi-blind deconvolution that re-optimizes the PSF undermines lens-quality interpretation: Eq. (3) jointly optimizes the WIRE network parameters theta, the PSF K, and the fixed-pattern noise F. Because K is a free variable, the deconvolved image quality is decoupled from the actual quality of the analytical PSF. This makes the Fig. 4 comparison effectively '(lens + reconstruction stack) yielding good imagery' rather than 'this lens has good imaging properties'. The fairness vs. the hyperboloid lens depends on whether the same reconstruction pipeline (with the same hyperparameters) is applied to both lenses; the paper does not state this. Whether the refractive lens images in Fig. 4 also receive this deconvolution is also unstated. As presented, an unfair comparison is plausible -- the meta-optic could win simply because the joint PSF optimization recovers more aggressively when the initial PSF is more diffuse.

Off-axis performance characterized only at 10 deg, far short of the imaging FOV: Optimization includes only 0 and 10 deg incidence angles. For the f/1 (NA 0.45) optic with the Boson 640 / FLIR A65 / FLIR A6751 sensors used (640x512 to 640x512 with 12-15 µm pitch), the diagonal half-FOV is approximately 25-31 deg, well beyond 10 deg. The PSF is not characterized off-axis past 10 deg, and the in-lab and in-the-wild figures do not separate center vs. corner sharpness. The Discussion advertises applications -- 'thermal scopes, perimeter security, UAVs' -- where corner-of-FOV performance matters. The paper should report the meta-optic's PSF or MTF as a function of field angle out to the sensor corner.

PSF characterization wavelength range (8.23-10.93 µm) does not cover the design band (8-12 µm): The QCL tunes from 8.23 to 10.93 µm but the design band is 8-12 µm and one of the imaging filter conditions is 12 +/- 0.25 µm. The PSF measurement therefore does not cover the 11-12 µm portion of the band, leaving the long-wavelength performance unmeasured. The broadband claim depends on uniform performance across the full band, so this gap should be filled (e.g., with a different QCL line, blackbody-illuminated narrowband measurements, or an explicit caveat).

Optical setup distance contradicts the formula for collimating-lens placement: With f_meta = 10 mm and f_2 = 15 mm: 2*f_meta + f_2 = 35 mm (correct for the first sentence) but f_meta + f_2 = 25 mm, not 35 mm (incorrect for the second sentence). The 35 mm distance from the meta-optic to the collimating lens cannot equal f_meta + f_2 with these focal lengths. Either the formula is wrong, or the distance is wrong; in either case the actual confocal alignment determines whether the post-collimating beam is parallel and how the PSF maps to the FPA. This is a real specification error in the characterization setup that should be corrected.

Robustness analysis lacks the magnitude of the fabrication-mimicking perturbation: The paper claims the design is robust to fabrication imperfections by injecting normally distributed perturbations into design parameters, but the standard deviation, distribution truncation, whether perturbations were applied during training (data augmentation) or only at evaluation, and whether they were applied to all parameters or a subset are not specified. The robustness claim is unverifiable as written, and is the primary bridge from simulation to expected fabricated performance.

Critical hyperparameters of optimization and deconvolution are missing: Reproduction is blocked by missing hyperparameters: the convergence threshold T, the maximum iteration count N, the SGD learning rate for the meta-optic optimization (only the DNN training rate is given), the cutoff frequencies (kx1, ky1), the perturbation standard deviation for the robustness check, the TV regularization weight eta_TV, the rank r of the fixed-pattern noise, and the WIRE iteration counts. Each is fixable independently; cumulatively they prevent reproduction of both the central simulated Strehl numbers and the deconvolved Fig. 4 imagery.

Equation (3) TV term and rank constraint underspecified; multiplicative FPN model deviates from cited prior work: Multiple specification problems with Eq. (3): (a) the TV term inside the sum, written as TV(N_theta(m,n)), depends on a single (m,n) but TV is conventionally a function of an entire image involving differences between neighboring pixels -- as written the equation is ill-defined; (b) the rank-constrained F is multiplicative (F * (K*N_theta)) rather than additive, but the cited prior work [32] models thermal fixed-pattern noise additively; the choice and its justification are not given; (c) the rank r is never specified. These together mean the headline 'in the wild' deconvolution is not reproducible.

Different image post-processing applied across panels confounds visual comparison: The in-lab pipeline (Section 4.4) applies background subtraction, contrast stretching, and block-matching denoising; the in-the-wild pipeline (Section 4.5) applies a different deconvolution stack; Section 2.4 says bandpass results are 'presented without any denoising' even though the broadband-result Fig. 3 caption notes 'after computation'. Whether the same processing is applied uniformly across the lenses being compared (especially the hyperboloid baseline and refractive lens) is not stated. As presented, post-processing differences could account for some of the visual quality differences claimed for the meta-optic.

Hyperboloid baseline at the same height/periodicity may be unfairly handicapped: The hyperboloid baseline is constrained to the same height and periodicity as the meta-optic under test, which may not be the design parameters that maximize hyperboloid performance. The hyperboloid is a monochromatic phase profile, and its performance depends on having a meta-atom library that spans 0-2pi at the design wavelength. Whether the simple-pillar library used for the hyperboloid spans full phase coverage at 10 µm (or whichever the chosen design wavelength is -- not stated), and whether a different library would have produced a stronger hyperboloid baseline, is not addressed. This bears on whether the 6x advantage is in part due to a weakened baseline.

Local phase approximation acknowledged but not quantified: The local phase approximation (LPA) is acknowledged as a limitation but not characterized. With Lambda = 4 µm and lambda spanning 8-12 µm, neighbor coupling is significant, and inverse-designed phase profiles tend to have abrupt transitions where LPA error is largest. Quoting a future fix without quantifying current LPA error -- e.g., by comparing LPA-based simulation to a full-wave simulation on a small representative region of the optic -- leaves uncertain how predictive the simulated 0.045 Strehl is of the fabricated lens.

DRIE-induced sidewall and CD imperfections at 10 µm depth not characterized: At 10 µm scatterer height with potentially sub-micron features in a 4 µm pitch, aspect ratios may exceed 10:1. DRIE introduces sidewall scalloping, draft angle, and bottom-corner rounding; these systematic deviations from the idealized binary geometry are not the same as the random Gaussian perturbation analysis in Sec 2.2. The minimum CD achieved on the fabricated optic, the measured sidewall angle, and the resulting deviation from the simulated transmission spectrum are not reported. This is the most likely real-world divergence between simulated 0.045 Strehl and what the lens actually delivers.

Trilayer hybridization conclusion does not properly subtract dielectric self-screening: The paper's own logic on dielectric self-screening implies the trilayer redshift should be larger than the heterobilayer redshift even in the absence of hybridization. In the HB, replacing one h-BN-like environment (epsilon ~ 4) with a TMD layer (epsilon ~ 13-16 by their own Table 1) produces a ~10 meV redshift. In a 2H trilayer, the central WSe2 layer has *two* adjacent TMD layers (one on each face) where there were h-BN-like environments before, so by the same screening logic the dielectric shift should be approximately 2x the HB value, i.e., ~20 meV -- already accounting for most of the observed 21 meV shift. The paper, however, treats the screening contribution to the trilayer as still ~10 meV and assigns the residual ~11 meV (and effectively all of the 21 meV) to hybridization. This is the load-bearing argument for the trilayer interpretation and is not airtight. A more careful treatment would either (a) explicitly model the depth of the screening environment to show that screening saturates with one neighboring layer, or (b) admit that screening and hybridization contribute comparably and that the data cannot cleanly disentangle them.

MoSe2 background dielectric epsilon_bg = 15.6 is roughly 2x the literature value cited by the paper itself: The reported background dielectric constants -- monolayer MoSe2 (15.6), MoSe2/WSe2 heterobilayer (13.6), and WSe2 trilayer (13.8) -- are roughly twice published far-field values. Li et al. (Phys. Rev. B 90, 205422 (2014)), the unnumbered final reference in the paper's own bibliography and the explicit benchmark plotted in Fig. 1b's inset, gives epsilon_bg(MoSe2) ~ 6-7 below the A-exciton and epsilon_1(WSe2) ~ 7 below 1.6 eV vs. the paper's 9.7. Within the same paper, monolayer WSe2 is 9.7 while WSe2 trilayer is 13.8 -- a 40 percent jump that is hard to reconcile with epsilon_bg being an intrinsic material constant. Together these patterns suggest that the PDM is absorbing geometric or substrate-related contributions into the fitted epsilon_bg, which would also propagate into systematic biases on gamma_{r,0} (oscillator strength) and on the absolute redshift values used to argue for screening vs. hybridization. The paper does not engage with this discrepancy at all.

20 nm screening-length claim is the spatial resolution itself, not a deconvolved physical bound: The screening length is a central physical claim of the paper (highlighted in the abstract, where it is even strengthened to 'few nanometers'). Yet the upper bound of 20 nm is simply the instrument resolution -- the measured profile width *is* the tip response width. To convert this into a real upper bound on a physical screening length, the measured edge profile must be deconvolved against an independently calibrated tip response function, and a chi-square analysis must rule out wider screening lengths beyond noise. The main text gives no such analysis: the line profile is shown qualitatively only, the resolution is quoted from a supplementary figure, and the deconvolution procedure (if any) is not described. The 20 nm 'upper bound' is therefore the limit of what the technique could possibly resolve, not a measurement of the screening length, and the abstract's 'few nanometers' phrasing is not supported anywhere in the body.

Lorentzian dielectric form (Eq. 1) is dimensionally and conventionally non-standard: Equation 1 has multiple issues that together prevent reproduction of the table values from the equation alone. (i) The standard 2D-exciton Lorentzian (e.g., Refs. 27, 29 cited by the authors) has an 'i' in the numerator coefficient and uses the running frequency omega rather than omega_0 in the prefactor; the form here lacks the 'i' and uses omega_0 instead. (ii) Units mix: omega and omega_0 must both be either rad/s or eV, but Table 1 reports them in meV and the prefactor c/(omega_0 d) is dimensionless only if omega_0 is in rad/s and d is in meters -- this conversion is never specified. (iii) The damping is reported as 'gamma_nr/2 + gamma_d' rather than the conventional gamma_r/2 + gamma_nr/2 + gamma_d, dropping the gamma_r/2 contribution to the optical-coherence dephasing. Combined, these issues mean a careful reader cannot independently verify whether the +/-0.2 meV uncertainty on gamma_{r,0} or the 233 fs lifetime follow from the equation or from a different form used in the SOM. The radiative-lifetime expression tau_0 = hbar/(2 gamma_{r,0}) also embeds a factor-of-2 convention not connected to the cited references' tau_0 = hbar/gamma_r convention.

Bright-exciton attribution is supported only by a single qualitative PL comparison with no Stokes-shift discussion: The conclusion that bright excitons dominate the s-SNOM response rests on (a) an in-plane vs. out-of-plane symmetry argument from Ref. 30 (with details in the SOM) and (b) a single qualitative comparison: 'PL peak ~1.66 eV, in close agreement with s-SNOM data' for WSe2, with no quoted PL uncertainty. Two issues compound here. First, PL emission is typically Stokes-shifted from absorption by 5-20 meV at room temperature (depending on doping, exciton-phonon coupling, biexciton/trion content), so a tighter quantitative comparison than 'about 1.66 eV' is needed to establish meV-level agreement with s-SNOM (where omega_0 = 1660 +/- 2 meV). Second, the symmetry argument suppresses dark excitons but does not rule out trion or biexciton contributions, which are also bright and which can shift the apparent omega_0 by several meV at room temperature in MoSe2 (and somewhat differently in WSe2). Neither alternative interpretation is addressed in the main text, and the corresponding cross-check for MoSe2 (Section 5) cites a different gated sample (Ref. 43) rather than same-sample PL.

WSe2 dielectric extracted by this work disagrees with Ref. 56, the paper's own benchmark: Fig. 1b is described as showing the dielectric function of monolayer WSe2 from Ref. 56 (Li et al., 2014). Li et al.'s result has epsilon_1 dropping from ~7 below 1.6 eV to negative values around 1.66 eV. The paper's own fit yields epsilon_bg = 9.7 -- a 30+ percent disagreement on the same material with the same far-field benchmark. Because the paper places Ref. 56 in Fig. 1b as a calibration target, the reader expects quantitative agreement; instead it is silently ~30 percent off. Compounding the issue, Ref. 56 is cited in the body but appears unnumbered at the very end of the bibliography (after the numbered list ends at Ref. 55), suggesting a bookkeeping error. The combination of citation issue and quantitative disagreement weakens the credibility of the absolute dielectric-function values.

150 fs vs. 233 fs radiative lifetime discrepancy with Ref. 33 is described as 'consistent': 233 fs (this work) versus 150 fs (Ref. 33) is a 55 percent disagreement. Calling them 'consistent' is an overstatement: the +/-14 percent uncertainty on gamma_{r,0} maps to roughly 200-280 fs, which still does not include 150 fs. Either the systematic uncertainty bar should be widened (e.g., to acknowledge 2D-vs-quasi-2D corrections, substrate effects, and the unknown h-BN thickness) or the disagreement should be acknowledged. As written, the comparison is presented as confirmation of a result that actually differs significantly from the cited experimental benchmark.

Heterobilayer redshift comparison does not specify whether the monolayer baseline is from the same field of view: The 10 meV redshift is calculated from HB resonances (1573 MoSe2, 1648 WSe2) versus monolayer values (1583 MoSe2, 1660 WSe2). It is not clear whether the monolayer reference values come from the *same* field of view (so the comparison is internal and self-consistent) or from a different FOV or sample (where 5-10 meV shifts from strain, doping, contamination, h-BN thickness, or terrace location are common). The redshift is only ~1.7 sigma significant given Table 1 uncertainties (sqrt(5^2 + 3^2) ~ 6 meV). For the central screening-length claim that follows, the baseline should be made explicit, and the same-sample monolayer measurement (which does exist in the same FOV per Fig. 1c) should be used.

Strain at h-BN terrace is not considered as alternative explanation for spatial heterogeneity: TMD excitons redshift under tensile strain by ~50 meV/percent for WSe2. When a TMD lies across an h-BN terrace, bending over the step produces localized strain (a few-nm-wide step can yield strain of order 0.1 percent, i.e., ~5 meV shift). The paper attributes the spatial variation in exciton energy across the HB-monolayer interface (Fig. 4c) entirely to dielectric screening. The h-BN terrace happens to be in the same field of view as the screening-length measurement, so this alternative (and not unrelated) source of redshift must at minimum be considered and excluded -- e.g., by showing the line profile away from the terrace, or by checking whether the AFM topography is locally flat at the location of the screening-length cut.

Heterobilayer Lorentzian sum fit does not address possible interlayer coupling or fit degeneracies: The HB fit assumes a simple sum of two independent Lorentzians, returning gamma_{r,0}(MoSe2) = 0.9 +/- 0.5 meV (60 percent uncertainty), gamma_{r,0}(WSe2) = 2.1 +/- 0.6 meV, and Gamma(WSe2) = 24 +/- 9 meV (40 percent uncertainty). With two Lorentzians ~75 meV apart but with widths summing to ~37 meV, the fit is partially degenerate: oscillator strength can be moved between peaks while shifting epsilon_bg with little change in the fit. Two consequences: (i) gamma_{r,0}(WSe2) jumping from 1.4 (1L) to 2.1 (HB) -- a 50 percent increase reported as if it were a real change -- could plausibly be a fit artifact, and (ii) charge-transfer or interlayer-exciton-mediated coupling between MoSe2 and WSe2 lines (which can produce non-Lorentzian / Fano features at the meV level) is not tested as an alternative. A 'two coupled oscillators' control fit would reassure readers that the 10 meV redshift survives model variation.

Abstract overstates novelty and capability relative to cited prior TEPL work and what was actually demonstrated: The paper's own Introduction acknowledges existing TEPL work on TMDs (Refs. 10-19) that achieves comparable or finer resolution -- Park et al. (Ref. 12) image dark excitons, Darlington et al. (Ref. 19) image strain-localized excitons in nanoscale bubbles, all at sub-20 nm scales. The 'previously unattainable 20 nm resolution' is therefore an overstatement; the actual novelty is the *combination* of nanoscale resolution with quantitative complex-dielectric-function extraction (epsilon_1 + i epsilon_2) for excitons, which TEPL does not provide. Separately, the conclusion claims this work 'lay[s] the groundwork for future spatio-temporal studies' of moire excitons and exciton phase transitions, but the work is purely CW and the 20 nm resolution is generally too coarse for the moire periodicities (~1-10 nm) the paper invokes. The abstract framing should be tightened to reflect the actual contribution.

Abstract claim of 'few nanometers' screening length is unsupported in the body: The body of the paper explicitly states that 'we conclude that our nano-IR scans yield only the upper bound estimate of this length scale limited by the spatial resolution of our method' (Section 6). The 'few nanometers' phrasing of the abstract has no support in the body -- the only number that appears is 20 nm (the resolution itself) or '~10 nm' from theoretical Ref. 9 (not measured in this work). This is a meaningful disagreement between abstract framing and what was measured: the abstract reads as if a length scale was determined, while the body acknowledges only an upper bound at the resolution.

Sample stack and h-BN thickness underspecified, blocking reproduction of the dielectric-function fits: The PDM inversion that yields all parameters in Table 1 depends on the substrate dielectric environment of the TMD: h-BN thickness, presence/absence of SiO2 beneath h-BN, the specific Si substrate, and any cap layer. None of these are specified. Standard PDM analysis (Refs. 30, 31 cited) was developed for graphene/SiO2 -- substrates much thicker than typical h-BN flakes. h-BN flakes in this kind of work are typically 20-50 nm thick on SiO2/Si, which is *not* in the 'thick substrate' limit and requires multilayer PDM. Whether a multilayer PDM was used, and what stack parameters entered the fit, is not stated. Without these details: (i) the fits in Table 1 are not reproducible; (ii) the +/-0.5 to +/-0.8 uncertainties on epsilon_bg cannot be evaluated against substrate-stack uncertainty; (iii) systematic differences from Ref. 56's far-field results (Issue: 'WSe2 dielectric vs. Ref. 56') cannot be attributed.

h-BN reference normalization is asserted to be frequency-independent without quantitative bound or control: The entire spectroscopic procedure normalizes by h-BN, so any residual frequency dependence of the h-BN near-field signal in 1.50-1.75 eV propagates directly into s_n(omega)/s_n(h-BN) and phi_n(omega) - phi_n(h-BN), and into the inferred dielectric function. Reference 25 is a general h-BN photonics review; the paper does not quote a measured upper bound on the h-BN signal variation across this band, nor does it report a control measurement (e.g., bare h-BN/SiO2 vs. photon energy on the actual sample). Without such a bound, claimed precisions of +/-2 to +/-6 meV on omega_0 and ~0.2-0.7 meV on the radiative rate are difficult to verify. Additionally, h-BN is anisotropic (epsilon_in-plane ~ 4.9, epsilon_out-of-plane ~ 3.0); the paper quotes a single value '~4' for screening arguments without specifying which component enters the analysis.

Spectra averaged over entire monolayer regions, in tension with the 20 nm resolution capability: All headline parameter values in Table 1 are derived from area-averaged near-field signals over an entire monolayer region. The paper emphasizes 'highly uniform response within regions occupied by each of the TMD materials' but never quantifies that uniformity. If edges, wrinkles, or contamination contribute systematically (as the introduction itself flags), the area average is biased. The same dataset is then used to argue for spatial-resolution-limited (20 nm) screening lengths -- which directly relies on intra-region heterogeneity being resolvable. These two narratives are in tension: either the response is uniform (and the 20 nm resolution adds little to the parameter determination) or it is heterogeneous (and the area-averaged Table 1 entries are mixing inhomogeneous responses). The main text never shows the per-pixel spread of fitted omega_0 within a single monolayer region.

Spatial resolution of 20 nm is not operationally defined or characterized in main text: The 20 nm figure is the central headline number (also driving the screening-length upper bound and the abstract's 'previously unattainable' claim) yet the main text gives no operational definition: 10-90 percent edge response? FWHM of a step convolution? Tip radius? It points only to a supplementary figure. Reusing this number as the screening-length upper bound means any ambiguity in how it was measured propagates into a physical claim. A standard 'edge response on a known sample' value, with the criterion stated in the main text, should be provided.

Tip illumination angle, polarization, and incident power not specified: Quantitative recovery of the in-plane dielectric function from s-SNOM signals depends on the incidence angle, the s/p polarization mix at the tip, and the tip-tapping amplitude (which combined with harmonic order sets the demodulation kernel). None of these are stated. Incident CW power matters too because TMDs at room temperature can heat or photogenerate trions/biexcitons, which would shift apparent omega_0 or broaden gamma_d. Without these parameters, the +/-2-6 meV resonance precisions cannot be benchmarked against systematic effects.

Fitting procedure (cost function, joint vs. separate amplitude/phase, error definition) entirely delegated to SOM: All headline numbers depend on a non-trivial PDM-based inverse fit, but the main text relegates *all* details to the SOM. At minimum, the body should specify: (i) what is fit (amplitude only, phase only, or jointly), (ii) which substrate parameters are assumed, (iii) the cost function used, and (iv) whether the errors in Table 1 are statistical fit uncertainties, systematic uncertainties (e.g., substrate stack), or some combination. Without this minimum, a reader cannot evaluate whether +/-0.5 to +/-9 meV uncertainties are meaningful, and the very large fractional uncertainties on the HB damping (24 +/- 9 meV) and HB MoSe2 radiative rate (0.9 +/- 0.5 meV) raise the suspicion of fit degeneracies.

PDM applicability to thin h-BN flakes (vs. thick SiO2 substrates) is not justified: References 30 and 31 develop the PDM for graphene/SiO2 and SiO2 thin films -- substrates much thicker than h-BN flakes used here. h-BN flakes for this kind of experiment are typically 20-50 nm thick on SiO2/Si, which is *not* in the 'thick substrate' limit. For h-BN of intermediate thickness, the underlying SiO2 (and even the Si reflection) contribute to the tip response. Whether a multilayer PDM was used, or whether the thick-h-BN approximation is justified for the actual sample stack, is not stated, and propagates into all extracted dielectric-function values.

Polariton-regime claim conflicts with cited Ref. 8 observation in WSe2: The paper claims polaritons cannot be reached at room T because epsilon_1 does not cross zero in their data, but then cites Ref. 8 (Sternbach et al.) which DID observe polaritons in WSe2 at room T using pump-probe to access excited-state Rydberg excitons. The 'notable exception' framing hand-waves past the question of whether the present technique could reproduce that result, or whether room-temperature ground-state polaritons are intrinsically forbidden vs. simply outside the present S/N. Additionally, the supporting reference (Ref. 36) is for cryogenic WS2, not WSe2, so the claim that 'reducing the damping rate' would access polaritons in WSe2 is not directly supported by the cited experiment.

MoSe2 epsilon_1 enhancement attributed to oscillator strength is largely driven by inflated epsilon_bg: In a Lorentzian, off-resonance epsilon_1 is dominated by epsilon_bg plus the integrated oscillator weight (proportional to gamma_{r,0}/omega_0). In Table 1, gamma_{r,0}(MoSe2) = 1.7 +/- 0.3 meV vs. gamma_{r,0}(WSe2) = 1.4 +/- 0.2 meV is only a 20 percent increase with overlapping error bars, but epsilon_bg jumps from 9.7 (WSe2) to 15.6 (MoSe2). Therefore most of the apparent 'enhancement' of epsilon_1 below resonance in MoSe2 is driven by the (implausibly high) MoSe2 epsilon_bg, not by oscillator strength. Attributing the enhancement to gamma_{r,0} is misleading.

Curled-finger training accuracies are inverted between MCA and SCA, contradicting the rest of the paper: Throughout the paper MCA is presented as superior to SCA (gesture training: MCA 100% vs SCA 99.2%; curled-finger 100-epoch recognition: MCA 98.2% vs SCA 69.7%). Yet on the same curled-finger task, training accuracies are reported as MCA 76.3% and SCA 99.8% — the opposite ordering. The very next sentence ('the discrepancies decreasing from 0.8% to 23.5%') is consistent with MCA leading by 23.5 pp (99.8-76.3), which strongly suggests the labels in the previous sentence are swapped. Furthermore, '0.8% to 23.5%' is described as 'decreasing' even though 23.5 > 0.8, compounding the editorial confusion. Because this passage is the headline edge-detection evidence, the inversion materially affects how a reader interprets the central application claim and must be corrected.

Imaging benchmark uses a commercial Melexis FPA, not the fabricated MCA detector — the headline 98.1% / 98.2% gains are software-vs-software comparisons: Section 'Multichannel infrared imaging' presents Fig 4 as evidence that the printable MCA enhances edge detection, and the abstract says 'shape classification (98.1%) and edge detection (98.2%) using our multichannel infrared images compared with single-channel detectors'. But the actual scenes are captured by a commercial Melexis 192x144 FPA, and the MCA / SCA outputs are then synthesized in OPENZYNQ from per-channel responsivity models. So the 98.1% / 98.2% numbers are obtained by two software pipelines on top of the same FPA, not by running the fabricated MCA against a fabricated SCA. The abstract and introduction phrasing leads readers to infer a hardware demonstration that did not happen, and any claim of 'faster training' carries the same caveat. This needs explicit acknowledgement in the abstract, results, and conclusions.

Comparison between MCA and SCA does not control for input-dimensionality, confounding 'spectral channels' with 'wider classifier input': MCA feeds a 6-channel-per-pixel tensor into the classifier; SCA feeds 1 channel per pixel. The classifier therefore sees 6x more features per spatial location with MCA, which alone explains faster convergence and higher small-sample accuracy even if every MCA channel were spectrally redundant. The standard control — replicating the SCA channel six times, or projecting MCA back to a single channel by averaging — is not run. Without this control, the gap (e.g., 33 pp at 10 epochs, 5 pp at 100 epochs) cannot be attributed to genuine spectral diversity. This confound undermines the central claim that the device's 'parallel processing' is what improves recognition, and it contaminates every numerical comparison in Fig 4 and the conclusions.

Imaging / simulation pipeline is described in two sentences; classifier architecture, dataset size, splits, and forward model are absent: The strongest application claim depends entirely on the imaging simulation, yet the main text gives no information about: (i) the classifier (architecture, depth, loss, optimizer, regularization, learning rate); (ii) the dataset (number of gesture images per class, number of curled-finger images, total size, class balance, subject hold-out); (iii) the train/val/test split; (iv) the forward model that converts a Melexis frame into per-channel MCA outputs (which channel-response curves are used? do they include device-to-device variability or only the average curve?); and (v) the OPENZYNQ commit / configuration. Combined with the missing dataset and code (see the data-availability comment), the 98.1% / 98.2% numbers are not independently reproducible.

Detection-band claim ('IR-C band, 3 microns to 1 mm') overstates the demonstrated operating window; biological-thermal claim has no passive measurement: Two compounding problems. (1) The phrase 'detection range within the IR-C band (3 μm to 1 mm)' is technically true (the operating window is a subset of IR-C), but reads as if the device covers the full band. The device's measured plasmon resonance peaks span ~1084-1292 cm^-1, i.e. ~7.7-9.2 microns; the laser used (Methods 'Measurements') tunes only 2.3-10 microns. (2) The text immediately leverages this to claim relevance to human thermal radiation in 8-14 microns, but no passive measurement (e.g., a warm body in front of the device with no laser) is reported; the photocurrent characterization always uses an active laser source < 1 mW. The pivot from 'this band overlaps biological thermal radiation' to 'our device can handle it' is therefore an inferential leap unsupported by the experiments shown.

'Epoch' is defined inconsistently: results paragraph says 3,600 iterations, Fig 4 captions say 1,000: The body of Section 'Multichannel infrared imaging' says each epoch is 3,600 iterations (and that gesture training reached its plateau 'after 3,600 iterations'). Fig 4 captions, however, state '100 epochs ... with each epoch consisting of 1,000 iterations' for both the gesture experiment (b, c) and the curled-finger experiment (d, e). Total training compute therefore differs by a factor of 3.6 depending on which definition is used, and the 'faster training speed' claim is unanchored. Either the body or the captions must be corrected.

Asymmetric contact-metal scheme is named inconsistently (Pd/Ti vs Au/Ti and Au/Ni) and the metals determine the zero-bias claim: Section 'Type-printing' says the asymmetric contacts are 20 nm Pd and 20 nm Ti capped with 80 nm Au. Methods 'Device fabrication' instead names 'Au/Ti and Au/Ni' as the source and drain in one sentence, then names 'Ti and Pd layers' in the very next sentence — three different metals (Ti, Ni, Pd) within one paragraph. The work-function asymmetry between source and drain is the physical origin of the zero-bias photocurrent, so the choice (Pd/Ti ~5.2/4.3 eV vs Ti/Ni ~4.3/5.0 eV) materially affects the central claim. The reader cannot determine which configuration was actually fabricated and characterized.

Stripe geometry: W (period), w (single-domain width), and d (in eqn 1) are used interchangeably across sections: Section 'Type-printing' defines W = period (200 nm-1 μm) and w = single-domain width (100-500 nm), with W = 2w. Eqn (1) uses a third variable d for 'ferroelectric superdomain width'. Fig 3a and Section 'Multichannel infrared imaging' both refer to 'a ferroelectric domain width' ranging '100 to 500 nm' for the MCA and 500 nm for the SCA — values that match w, not W. Because eqn (1) uses q ~ N pi/d, whether d is the period or the single-domain width changes predicted plasmon frequencies by a factor of ~2. The notation must be reconciled across the paper.

POG-to-E_F conversion (mu_c = +121 meV upward, -448 meV downward) is asserted with no value of alpha' or pristine baseline: These chemical potentials drive the FEM simulation in Fig 2j-k and the predicted spectrum from eqn (1). They are derived from POG values 1586 cm^-1 (upward) and 1597 cm^-1 (downward), an 11 cm^-1 splitting. Converting that to E_F requires the integral constant alpha'; ref 29 gives a specific numerical value but the paper neither states alpha' nor identifies the pristine-graphene reference POG. The asymmetry |+121|:|-448| ~ 1:3.7 implies a substantial baseline shift between 'upward' and 'pristine' graphene, but that baseline is never stated in the main text. Without alpha' and the reference POG, the chemical potentials — and the simulation built on them — cannot be reproduced.

Photoresponsivity '~30 mA/W' is reported without wavelength, illumination intensity, device area, or per-cell breakdown: Responsivity for graphene plasmonic detectors depends sensitively on wavelength, illumination intensity (laser spot vs uniform flood), device active area, and operating temperature. The text reports a single rounded value, doesn't say which of the six MCA cells produced it, doesn't give the spot size (only that laser power < 1 mW), and doesn't normalize for area. Comparison plots in Fig 3e against refs 31-34 — including waveguide-integrated graphene detectors with multi-A/W responsivities — therefore cannot be evaluated for fairness. The conclusions section then drops the 'comparable, not highest' qualifier and calls 30 mA/W 'high', which compounds the issue.

Number of usable spectral channels is unclear; six cells share only ~200 cm^-1 of tuning with no FWHM or cross-talk reported: The MCA pixel is described as 6-channel, but six resonance peaks span only 1084-1292 cm^-1 (~16% relative tuning). Typical graphene plasmonic linewidths in this regime are 50-100 cm^-1 (refs 13, 15), so adjacent peaks likely overlap heavily. The paper reports neither per-channel FWHM nor a measured cross-talk matrix. Because the 'six channels per pixel' framing supports the claim of replacing multi-grating / multi-camera systems, the practical channel count needs explicit characterization.

Numerical-simulations Methods paragraph defers all configuration details (RPA gamma, FEM mesh, BFO eps_r, OPENZYNQ classifier) to the supplement: Three different simulation chains are central to the paper's results. The Methods main-text covers them in three sentences and refers all parameters to supplementary sections: RPA scattering rate / temperature / Fermi velocity, FEM mesh resolution, BFO permittivity (eps_r), substrate boundary conditions, OPENZYNQ classifier architecture and training hyperparameters. Even acknowledging that supplements exist, key parameters that materially shift omega_spr (eps_r, gamma) and the test accuracies (classifier choice) belong in the main text given how prominently the simulation results are featured.

Dataset, code, and trained-model availability is too thin to support reproducibility of ML claims: The paper points to a public OPENZYNQ repo for the simulation framework but does not link a specific commit, the gesture/curled-finger image dataset, the trained-model weights, or the training scripts.
